To examine these factors, incarcerated participants completed the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ), assessing perceptions of autonomy, safety, relationships, and opportunities within prison (Bosma et al., 2020).
table.formatted: To examine these factors, incarcerated participants completed the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ), assessing perceptions of autonomy, safety, relationships, and opportunities within prison <ref type="bibr">(Bosma et al., 2020)</ref>.

table.text: Only men were recruited to the prisoner groups.
All eligible candidates received oral and written information and provided written informed consent.

For incarcerated participants, consent procedures were conducted without staff present to minimize perceived links with the judicial system, and participants were explicitly informed of the research team's independence from the penitentiary and judicial system.
On average, outgoing participants had spent 1,378 days in detention (SD = 1,411).
Incoming participants were significantly younger than outgoing participants (t = -2.34, p = .027).
Incoming participants were relatively evenly distributed across remand/pre-trial detention (37.9%), sentences of 1-3 years (20.7%), 3-5 years (20.7%), and 5-10 years (20.7%).
In contrast, outgoing participants were predominantly serving longer sentences, with 69.2% reporting sentence lengths of 5-10 years.
The most frequently reported types of offence in incoming participants were violent offences (27.6%), followed by drug-related, non-violent property and sexual offences (24.1% each).
During the encoding phase (Fig. 2A), participants were introduced to four fictional characters: two with incarceration experience and two without.

table.text: Narratives were randomized across sessions so that all five narratives per group were presented across the longitudinal follow-up.

Stimuli represented ethnic diversity, with character's ethnicity (Afro-descent or European descent) alternating across sessions so that all participants were exposed to both ethnic groups across the longitudinal assessment.

After the encoding phase, participants completed memory checks requiring them to match narratives with the corresponding faces to ensure they correctly remembered the identity of the characters (Fig. 2B).

To facilitate longitudinal follow-up, participants provided contact details on paper-based forms.
Participants still in prison were contacted through institutional channels, whereas released participants were contacted using the information provided at baseline.
Incoming participants were notified of upcoming follow-up sessions through letters sent via the prison communication system (Prison Cloud) or via institutional intermediaries.
At approximately 3 months post-release, participants were contacted to schedule follow-up assessments.
In contrast, for outgoing participants, all participants were sentenced and nearing release, making this distinction less relevant.

Participants were recruited across 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium, which varied in security level, regime, and capacity.

Participants were not originally excluded if they had a mental disorder, however those who experienced active psychosis during testing, who were transferred to a psychiatric unit, who were unable to complete the task, or who were non-compliant were excluded.

When release was delayed by up to six months beyond baseline, the second assessment was conducted while participants were still incarcerated (n=2), although this assessment was not included in the final analyses.
Most incoming participants were recruited from Brugge (31.0%), Jamioulx (20.7%), and Tournai (20.7%), followed by Nieuw Dendermonde (17.2%), Turnhout (6.9%), and Marche-en-Famenne (3.4%).

Outgoing participants were primarily recruited from Leuven Centraal (38.5%), while smaller proportions were recruited from Beveren (15.4%), Ittre (15.4%), and Leuze (15.4%), and few participants from Ruiselede Agricultural Correctional Facility (7.7%) and Saint-Hubert Detention Center (7.7%).
Age Incoming participants were significantly younger than outgoing participants.
Incoming participants had a mean age of 35.97 years (SD = 11.89), whereas outgoing participants had a mean age of 44.62 years (SD = 10.70).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants Three hundred and fifty (N = 350) male prisoners from 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium participated in the study. Only men were recruited to the prisoner groups. Women make up roughly 4% of the Belgian prison population (World Prison Brief, 2024) and are held in only a small number of establishments. Therefore, recruiting women would have introduced bias on gender, and their concentration in a few prisons would have confounded gender with prison site. The prisoner groups were therefore restricted to men. The study protocol was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) on August 10, 2023 (DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/M4TS9). Power analyses with G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) for the Group (2level: Incoming/Outgoing) × Session (3-level) × Scenario (2-level: Pro-/Anti-Social) interactions, using a repeated-measures approximation, indicated a total target sample size of 28 participants (14 per group) to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25) with 95% power.
table.statistical_test_other: repeated-measures ANOVA approximation for Group × Session × Scenario interaction

table.text: However, G*Power misspecifies designs that combine between-and within-subject interactions(Brysbaert, 2019), and our confirmatory analyses used linear mixed-effects models (LMM). Therefore, additional simulation-based power analyses were conducted for the actual model. This analysis was not part of the preregistered plan and is reported as a deviation (see Supplementary S1). To avoid circularity, the assumed effect size was fixed independently of the observed results. Simulating the Group × Session × Scenario interaction on the binomial choice model (64 free-choice trials per scenario per session), and assuming a small interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) with moderate between-participant variability in the session change, 80% power was reached at approximately 30 participants per group. Main effects and lower-order interactions required fewer participants. Because longitudinal prison research entails high attrition, baseline recruitment targets were set substantially higher than these completing-sample targets. Details on sample size estimation, recruitment and inclusion/exclusion criteria are provided in Supplementary S1.

The preregistered sample-size target was derived from an a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) (medium effect, f = .25, 95% power). Because G*Power approximates such designs as repeatedmeasures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions combining between-and within-subject factors (Brysbaert, 2019), and because the confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models, an additional simulation-based power analysis was conducted for the design actually used. This analysis was not preregistered and was performed after data collection. To avoid circularity, the effect size was set by convention rather than from the observed estimates. For each candidate sample size, datasets from a binomial GLMM were simulated with the full Group × Session × Scenario structure, a by-participant random intercept and random slopes for Session and Scenario, and 64 free-choice trials per scenario per session (aggregated to binomial counts within each participant × session × scenario cell).

The preregistered sample-size target was derived from an a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) (medium effect, f = .25, 95% power). Because G*Power approximates such designs as repeatedmeasures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions combining between-and within-subject factors (Brysbaert, 2019), and because the confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models, an additional simulation-based power analysis was conducted for the design actually used. This analysis was not preregistered and was performed after data collection. To avoid circularity, the effect size was set by convention rather than from the observed estimates. For each candidate sample size, datasets from a binomial GLMM were simulated with the full Group × Session × Scenario structure, a by-participant random intercept and random slopes for Session and Scenario, and 64 free-choice trials per scenario per session (aggregated to binomial counts within each participant × session × scenario cell).

Assuming a small interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) and moderate between-participant variability in the session change (random-slope SD = 0.4 on the logit scale), 80% power for the threeway interaction was reached at approximately 30 participants per group in the present longitudinal design (two groups × three sessions). Main effects and lower-order interactions reached 80% power at smaller samples. The achieved longitudinal samples met the requirement for incoming participants (n = 34 with complete behavioural data; n = 29 with usable EEG across all three sessions) but fell below it for outgoing participants (n = 13 and n = 11, respectively); accordingly, null effects in the outgoing group are interpreted using equivalence tests as inconclusive rather than as evidence of absence (see Results).

table.title: Effect of Imprisonment Intergroup Bias in Pro/Antisocial Decision-Making: A Longitudinal EEG Study of Newly-detained and Newly-released Prisoners.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.manipulated_variables: We will manipulate the scenarios, the fictional characters and the duo presented.
table.missing_data_handling: If data are missing on questionnaires, we will replace the missing data by using a multivariate imputation by chained equations algorithm (MICE) which models each feature with missing values as a function of all the other variables, and uses that prediction estimate for imputation (Pedregosa et al., 2011).
table.additional_comments: This study is part of a larger project investigating the changes in executive functions induced by imprisonment and the differential impact of prison regimes. The protocol aims at answering several additional research questions, regarding emotion recognition ability, cognitive control, sensitivity to reward and punishment and anti-social behaviour.
table.research_questions:
•	It has been repeatedly shown that perceiving an individual as an outgroup member tends to reduce prosociality towards that individual compared to ingroup members (Stürmer et al., 2005, Hein et al., 2010, Pech et al., 2022), an effect that has been referred to as the intergroup prosociality bias. Indeed, prisoners are biased towards intergroup prosociality, as they display behaviors consistent with in-group favoritism (Balafoutas et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). However, given the absence of longitudinal evidence and the heterogeneity in identification with the inmate group, we formulate bidirectional hypotheses regarding changes in intergroup behavior over time.
H1.A : For individuals entering prison (incoming group), incarceration may either strengthen or weaken intergroup bias. Specifically, over the course of 8 months, prisoners may (a) show progressively reduced prosocial behavior toward outgroup individuals (i.e. who have never been incarcerated) and increased prosocial behavior toward ingroup individuals (i.e. who currently are or have been incarcerated), alongside increased antisocial behavior toward outgroup individuals and decreased antisocial behavior toward ingroup individuals; or (b) exhibit the opposite pattern, reflecting reduced identification with the inmate group.
H1.B : For individuals leaving prison (outgoing group), changes in intergroup bias following release may also be bidirectional. Over the course of 8 months after release, former prisoners may (a) show increased prosocial behavior toward outgroup individuals and decreased prosocial behavior toward ingroup individuals, alongside decreased antisocial behavior toward outgroup individuals and increased antisocial behavior toward ingroup individuals; or (b) maintain or reinforce ingroup-oriented patterns, depending on their level of identification with the inmate group and their reintegration context.

•	Choosing between an individual from an outgroup (i.e., someone one does not identify with) and an ingroup (i.e., someone one identifies with) involves cognitive conflict (Pech & Caspar, 2022; Pech et al., 2022). Previous EEG studies have shown that participants experience greater conflict, as indexed by increased midfrontal theta power, when selecting an outgroup individual over an ingroup individual in prosocial contexts, suggesting that prosocial behavior toward outgroup members may be less intuitive (Pech & Caspar, 2022; Pech et al., 2022).
H2.A : At the neural level, we will examine how cognitive conflict associated with prosocial and antisocial decisions evolves over time in both incoming (during incarceration) and outgoing (after release) individuals. Given the absence of longitudinal evidence in these populations, and the paradigm including antisocial decisions being new, we formulate bidirectional hypotheses. Specifically, we predict that over time, individuals may exhibit either an increase or a decrease in cognitive conflict when making antisocial or prosocial decisions, as reflected by changes in midfrontal theta activity.
H2.B : In addition, we hypothesize that cognitive conflict will differ depending on whether decisions target ingroup or outgroup individuals. However, because group identification may vary substantially across individuals and across time (e.g., during incarceration vs. reintegration), we adopt a bidirectional hypothesis for both groups. That is, antisocial decisions may become either more or less conflictual when directed toward outgroup compared to ingroup individuals, and similarly, prosocial decisions toward outgroup members may elicit either increased or decreased conflict over time, in both groups.
H2.C : Importantly, we expect that these effects may follow different trajectories in incoming and outgoing groups. In incoming individuals, incarceration may alter the salience of ingroup–outgroup distinctions, whereas in outgoing individuals, these effects may persist, diminish, or reverse during reintegration. Overall, this approach allows us to test whether changes in cognitive conflict reflect adaptation to the prison environment, disengagement from it, or individual differences in social identification.
table.study_design_overview:
The study is a repeated-measures design with time as a within-subject factor (Baseline, 4 months, 8 months). Participants include both incoming detainees assessed shortly after incarceration and outgoing detainees assessed prior to release, recruited from French and Flemish prisons in Belgium. In addition, a community control group is included to account for repeated task exposure effects, with one 4-month interval re-test only. Incoming participants are recruited within the first three to seven weeks following incarceration, whereas outgoing participants are assessed a month prior to release. All incoming and outgoing participants are followed longitudinally at 4- and 8-month intervals.
Participants complete a modified version of the intended prosociality task (Pech et al., 2022), lasting approximately 20 minutes. During this task, participants are introduced to four fictional characters: two representing an ingroup (individuals with current or past incarceration experience) and two representing an outgroup (individuals without incarceration experience and from a different socio-economic background). At the beginning of the task, participants rate the extent to which they identify with each character.
Participants are then presented with a series of prosocial and antisocial scenarios, followed by a pair of characters. These pairs either consist of either one ingroup and one outgroup member (free-choice condition) or two individuals from the same group (forced-choice condition). For each trial, participants decide toward which individual they would direct the prosocial or antisocial action.
Behavioral measures include the proportion of choices directed toward ingroup versus outgroup individuals (separately for prosocial and antisocial contexts) and reaction times for each decision. Neural activity is recorded throughout the task using electroencephalography (EEG).
Behavioral and neural data are analyzed at the trial level using linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models ((G)LMMs), accounting for the hierarchical structure of the data (trials nested within participants) and variability in the number of observations across groups. Neural analyses focus on response-locked midfrontal theta power as index of cognitive conflict. Behavioral analyses examine choice patterns using the same set of predictors, including decision type (prosocial vs. antisocial), session, and group (incoming, outgoing).
table.randomization: The order of scenario and of the pairs displayed, and therefore the order of the forced and free condition, will be randomized across participants and across sessions to minimize order effects. The assignment of fictional characters is also randomized across participants. Across sessions, scenarios are randomly sampled from a predefined pool, such that participants are exposed to overlapping but not identical sets of scenarios over time.
table.data_collection_procedures:
As part of this study, incoming detainees, outgoing detainees, and community control participants will be recruited. Incoming participants will consist of newly detained prisoners, selected from weekly lists of individuals newly received into custody in French and Flemish prisons in Belgium. Outgoing participants will consist of prisoners approaching release. During recruitment periods, we will aim to approach all eligible detainees and invite them to participate, with recruitment timing adapted to institutional and logistical constraints.
Community control participants will consist of first-year psychology students from Ghent University, recruited via the SONA system. Control participants will complete the same task at each timepoint and will receive course credits for their participation.
Prisoners will be excluded if they were transferred from other establishments, are scheduled for deportation or awaiting extradition (incoming group), or if they have insufficient understanding of Dutch or French, present visual or motor impairments, or exhibit inappropriate behavior toward the researcher.
Baseline assessments (T1) will take place in prison, three to seven weeks after incarceration for incoming participants and prior to release for outgoing participants. Follow-up testing sessions will be conducted at 4 (T2) and 8 months (T3) after baseline assessment. Control participants will be assessed at the first 2 sessions only (4-month re-test).
At each assessment, comprehensive contact information will be collected, reviewed, and updated for detainees, including residential address, mobile phone number, email address, and, when available, social media contact details. Participants will also be asked to provide contact information for alternative contacts (e.g., family members or friends) and to consent to being recontacted through these intermediaries if necessary for follow-up assessments.
Participants will not be excluded based on the presence of mental disorders at recruitment. However, if participants are unable to complete the task or are non-compliant, they may be excluded from the analyses.
Participants will receive compensation for their participation. Incoming detainees will be compensated via their prison bank account. Outgoing participants will be compensated via bank transfer. Control participants will receive course credits for their participation at each timepoint.
table.sample_size: The target sample size for this study across all groups (control, incoming and outgoing) is approximatively 30 total participants completing the full study. Considering the high rates of attrition in studies involving prisoners with long periods of follow-up (Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Hassan et al., 2011; Lennox et al., 2013), we seek to recruit 300 incoming and 300 outgoing participants for the baseline assessment. For the control group we only seek to recruit 60 participants at baseline.
table.sample_size_rationale:
The target sample size was determined based on a series of a priori power analyses conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007), reflecting the different components of the study design.
First, a power analysis was conducted for the incarcerated groups only, including incoming and outgoing detainees. This analysis used a mixed repeated-measures framework with 2 groups and 6 repeated measurements, reflecting the combination of the 3-level session factor and the 2-level scenario factor. For detecting a medium effect size (f = .25), with 95% power, the required total sample size was estimated at 28 participants (i.e. 14 per group). 
Second, an additional power analysis included the community control group for additional analyses of practice effects. Because control participants were assessed at two sessions, this analysis used a mixed repeated-measures framework with 3 groups and 4 repeated measurements, corresponding to the 2-level session factor and the 2-level scenario factor. Under the same assumptions, the required total sample size was estimated at 45 participants (i.e. 15 per group).
However, this project is part of a larger study for which, keeping all other factors constant, an additional power analysis was conducted focusing on within-subject effects across 3 sessions, with 2 conditions (i.e. each task of the study includes at least 2 conditions), and was performed separately within each detainee group. This analysis yielded a required sample size of 28 participants per group.
Given the high attrition expected in longitudinal prison research, substantially larger samples are recruited at baseline to ensure sufficient statistical power at follow-up.
table.measured_variables:
•	The primary behavioral outcome variable is the choice, operationalized as the frequency of selecting ingroup versus outgroup individuals in the free-choice condition, separately for prosocial and antisocial scenarios.
•	At the neural level, theta band power will be measured using EEG. Theta activity will be examined both in response to the presentation of the scenarios and the choice options (stimulus-locked activity), and in response to the participants’ decision (response-locked activity). Analyses will compare theta power as a function of decision type (prosocial vs. antisocial), target (ingroup vs. outgroup), choice condition (free vs. forced), and across sessions.
•	Reaction time (RT) will be included as a covariate in the analyses, as an index of decision processes (e.g., conflict or deliberation), rather than as a primary outcome variable.
•	Demographic variables will be collected, including age, gender, level of education, nature of the offense(s) leading to incarceration, length of incarceration, past criminal records, and socio-economic status.
•	Personality and mental health measures will be included by means of self-reported questionnaires. Participants will rate each item based on its applicability over the preceding four weeks.
•	For incarcerated participants, perception of the prison environment will be assessed at baseline using the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ; Bosma et al., 2020), a validated instrument measuring perceived prison conditions and social relationships within the institution.
•	Following release (from T2 onwards), quality of life will be assessed using the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ; Harper et al., 2021), which is adapted to measure well-being and life conditions outside the prison environment.
table.statistical_tests:
We will analyze the dependent variables using mixed-effects models to account for the repeated-measures structure of the data and the hierarchical organization of trials nested within participants.
Behavioral outcomes will be analyzed at the trial level using generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) with a binomial link function. For the main confirmatory analysis, fixed effects will include Group (2-level), Session (3-level), Scenario (2-level), and their interactions. For the practice effect analysis, fixed effects will include Group (3-level), Session (2-level), Scenario (2-level), and their interactions.
Neural outcomes (theta band power) will be analyzed using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs). Fixed effects will include Group, Session, Scenario, and their interactions. Analyses will be restricted to the forced-choice condition to ensure an equal number of trials across conditions.
For both behavioral and neural analyses, covariates will include reaction time (RT), character identification ratings, age, and questionnaire-derived measures (e.g., PCQ, GLQ, mental health, personality), as well as relevant demographic variables such as gender, education level, socioeconomic status, criminal history, and characteristics of the offense. 
Random effects will include participant-level random intercepts, as well as random slopes for within-subject factors (e.g., Session and Scenario), where appropriate to capture individual variability in longitudinal changes and decision processes.
When significant main effects or interactions are observed, post-hoc pairwise comparisons will be conducted using estimated marginal means (EMMs), with appropriate correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Tukey adjustment).
Model assumptions will be assessed through standard diagnostic procedures, including inspection of residual distributions and evaluation of model fit.
table.transformations: Raw EEG data will be preprocessed. We will use a Biosemi 32-electrode EEG system with four external electrodes. Two of the external electrodes will be placed on the left and right mastoids. Data will be acquired using ActiveView software, and subsequently converted to BIDS format. To filter and clean the data, we will use MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013). The data will be re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST). For time–frequency analyses, data will be band-pass filtered between 1 and 40 Hz. Since our participants will not be placed in a Faraday Cage, we will apply a Notch filter to remove the power line noise at 50 Hz. To remove ocular and muscular artifacts, Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Artifact-related components will be identified using a combination of automatic classification and visual inspection of component topographies and time courses, and subsequently removed.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p<.05 criteria to determine the statistical significance of the ANOVA and post-hoc tests results. The post-hoc tests will be corrected for multiple comparisons using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjustment approach.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Outliers will be identified at the trial level using a within-participant 2-of-3 rule, combining three criteria: median absolute deviation (MAD > 3), z-score (|z| > 3), and interquartile range (IQR beyond 1.5 × IQR). Trials flagged by at least two of these criteria will be excluded from subsequent analyses.
EEG data will be excluded when excessive artifacts are present. Artifact rejection will be based on a combination of automated detection procedures and visual inspection. Trials contaminated by noise (e.g., due to eye movements, muscle activity, or signal instability) will be removed. Participants contributing an insufficient number of valid trials after preprocessing will be excluded from EEG analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses:
In the case where some prisoners are released before the end of the data collection period, we might include data from these participants and analyze it using a within-subject design. 
Scores on questionnaires assessing mental health, personality, and the quality of life inside and outside prison assessed using the PCQ and the GLQ respectively, will be compared over time to evaluate the effect of prison and time spent in prison on these factors.

•\tFollowing release (from T2 onwards), quality of life will be assessed using the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ; Harper et al., 2021), which is adapted to measure well-being and life conditions outside the prison environment.", "We will analyze the dependent variables using mixed-effects models to account for the repeated-measures structure of the data and the hierarchical organization of trials nested within participants.
Behavioral outcomes will be analyzed at the trial level using generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) with a binomial link function. For the main confirmatory analysis, fixed effects will include Group (2-level), Session (3-level), Scenario (2-level), and their interactions. For the practice effect analysis, fixed effects will include Group (3-level), Session (2-level), Scenario (2-level), and their interactions.
Neural outcomes (theta band power) will be analyzed using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs). Fixed effects will include Group, Session, Scenario, and their interactions. Analyses will be restricted to the forced-choice condition to ensure an equal number of trials across conditions.
For both behavioral and neural analyses, covariates will include reaction time (RT), character identification ratings, age, and questionnaire-derived measures (e.g., PCQ, GLQ, mental health, personality), as well as relevant demographic variables such as gender, education level, socioeconomic status, criminal history, and characteristics of the offense.
Random effects will include participant-level random intercepts, as well as random slopes for within-subject factors (e.g., Session and Scenario), where appropriate to capture individual variability in longitudinal changes and decision processes.
When significant main effects or interactions are observed, post-hoc pairwise comparisons will be conducted using estimated marginal means (EMMs), with appropriate correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Tukey adjustment).
Model assumptions will be assessed through standard diagnostic procedures, including inspection of residual distributions and evaluation of model fit.", "Raw EEG data will be preprocessed. We will use a Biosemi 32-electrode EEG system with four external electrodes. Two of the external electrodes will be placed on the left and right mastoids. Data will be acquired using ActiveView software, and subsequently converted to BIDS format. To filter and clean the data, we will use MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013). The data will be re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST). For time–frequency analyses, data will be band-pass filtered between 1 and 40 Hz. Since our participants will not be placed in a Faraday Cage, we will apply a Notch filter to remove the power line noise at 50 Hz. To remove ocular and muscular artifacts, Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Artifact-related components will be identified using a combination of automatic classification and visual inspection of component topographies and time courses, and subsequently removed.", "We will use the standard p<.05 criteria to determine the statistical significance of the ANOVA and post-hoc tests results. The post-hoc tests will be corrected for multiple comparisons using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjustment approach.", "Outliers will be identified at the trial level using a within-participant 2-of-3 rule, combining three criteria: median absolute deviation (MAD > 3), z-score (|z| > 3), and interquartile range (IQR beyond 1.5 × IQR). Trials flagged by at least two of these criteria will be excluded from subsequent analyses.
EEG data will be excluded when excessive artifacts are present. Artifact rejection will be based on a combination of automated detection procedures and visual inspection. Trials contaminated by noise (e.g., due to eye movements, muscle activity, or signal instability) will be removed. Participants contributing an insufficient number of valid trials after preprocessing will be excluded from EEG analyses.", "In the case where some prisoners are released before the end of the data collection period, we might include data from these participants and analyze it using a within-subject design.
Scores on questionnaires assessing mental health, personality, and the quality of life inside and outside prison assessed using the PCQ and the GLQ respectively, will be compared over time to evaluate the effect of prison and time spent in prison on these factors.", "input")), row.names = c("template_name", "title", "id", "link", "date_created", "date_modified", "date_registered", "embargo_end_date", "ia_url", "study_type", "blinding", "existing_data", "manipulated_variables", "missing_data_handling", "additional_comments", "research_questions", "study_design_overview", "randomization", "data_collection_procedures", "sample_size", "sample_size_rationale", "measured_variables", "statistical_tests", "transformations", "inference_criteria", "data_exclusion_criteria", "exploratory_analyses", "paper_id" ), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of deviations from preregistrations, see: van den Akker O, Bakker M, van Assen M, Pennington C, Verweij L, Elsherif M, Claesen A, Gaillard S, Yeung S, Frankenberger J, Krautter K, Cockcroft J, Kreuer K, Evans T, Heppel F, Schoch S, Korbmacher M, Yamada Y, Albayrak-Aydemir N, Wicherts J (2024). “The potential of preregistration in psychology: Assessing preregistration producibility and preregistration-study consistency.” Psychological Methods. doi:10.1037/met0000687. report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps ≥ .096", "p ≤ .016", "ps ≥ .131", 
"ps ≥ .095", "ps ≥ .536", "ps ≤ .004", "ps ≥ .09", "p > .05", 
"p < .05"), Text = c("No other main effect or interaction involving Session or Group were significant (all ps ≥ .096).", 
"Equivalence tests indicated that session-to-session differences in identification were statistically equivalent to zero within ±0.5 rating points (all session 403 contrasts ≤ 0.17 points; TOST p ≤ .016), supporting stable identification with incarceration-404 history targets across sessions rather than a failure to detect change.", 
"No other main effect or interaction involving Session 412 or Group were significant (all ps ≥ .131).", 
"No other session contrasts reached 416 significance among incoming participants (all ps ≥ .095).", 
"Outgoing participants showed no 417 significant longitudinal changes in either prosocial or antisocial scenarios (all ps ≥ .536).", 
"Across 419 all groups and sessions, participants consistently showed lower odds of choosing community 420 targets in antisocial relative to prosocial scenarios (all ps ≤ .004).", 
"The effects of Target (p = . 685) and decision time (p = . 112), and all interactions (all ps ≥ .09), were not significant.", 
"The absence of an overall group difference in social choices and the absence of a group-specific longitudinal FMθ change (Group × Session) in outgoing participants were not statistically equivalent to zero (TOST p > .05).", 
"An effect is equivalent to zero when TOST p < .05, equivalently when the 90% CI falls entirely within the equivalence bounds."
)), row.names = c(NA, -9L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 16 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: Education levels did not differ significantly between groups (p = .762) with the majority of both incoming and outgoing participants reporting secondary education (58.6% and 53.8%, respectively), whereas smaller proportions reported no formal education, primary education, or higher education.
Re-incarceration rates did not differ significantly between incoming and outgoing participants (U = 164.0, p = .498).
No other main effect or interaction involving Session or Group were significant (all ps ≥ .096).
No other main effect or interaction involving Session 412 or Group were significant (all ps ≥ .131).
No other session contrasts reached 416 significance among incoming participants (all ps ≥ .095).
Outgoing participants showed no 417 significant longitudinal changes in either prosocial or antisocial scenarios (all ps ≥ .536).

table.formatted: DT were significantly longer 421 for community target choices (β = 0.06, p < .001), whereas age was not a significant predictor 422 (p = .903).
table.expanded: DT were significantly longer 421 for community target choices (β = 0.06, p < .001), whereas age was not a significant predictor 422 (p = .903).
The effects of Target (p = . 685) and decision time (p = . 112), and all interactions (all ps ≥ .09), were not significant.

table.formatted: The absence of an overall group difference in social choices and the absence of a group-specific longitudinal FMθ change (Group × Session) in outgoing participants were not statistically equivalent to zero (TOST p > .05).
table.expanded: The absence of an overall group difference in social choices and the absence of a group-specific longitudinal FMθ change (Group × Session) in outgoing participants were not statistically equivalent to zero (TOST p > .05).
In contrast, the Session effect was reduced to non-significance when outliers were retained (F(2, 40.1) = 2.87, p = .068) and is therefore interpreted with caution (Supplementary S8).

table.header: S8. Sensitivity of the Neural Analyses to Outlier-trial Removal
table.expanded: The main effect of Session, by contrast, was reduced to non-significance (F(2, 40.1) = 2.87, p = .068), indicating that the session-related decline observed in the primary analysis was not robust to outlier retention.
A non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test indicated no significant difference between incoming and outgoing participants (p = .762).
The number of incarcerations did not differ significantly between incoming and outgoing participants, as indicated by a non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test (U = 164.0, p = .498).

live_data_statements: To examine these factors, incarcerated participants completed the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ), assessing perceptions of autonomy, safety, relationships, and opportunities within prison (Bosma et al., 2020).
Only men were recruited to the prisoner groups.
All eligible candidates received oral and written information and provided written informed consent.

For incarcerated participants, consent procedures were conducted without staff present to minimize perceived links with the judicial system, and participants were explicitly informed of the research team's independence from the penitentiary and judicial system.
On average, outgoing participants had spent 1,378 days in detention (SD = 1,411).
Incoming participants were significantly younger than outgoing participants (t = -2.34, p = .027).
Incoming participants were relatively evenly distributed across remand/pre-trial detention (37.9%), sentences of 1-3 years (20.7%), 3-5 years (20.7%), and 5-10 years (20.7%).
In contrast, outgoing participants were predominantly serving longer sentences, with 69.2% reporting sentence lengths of 5-10 years.
The most frequently reported types of offence in incoming participants were violent offences (27.6%), followed by drug-related, non-violent property and sexual offences (24.1% each).
During the encoding phase (Fig. 2A), participants were introduced to four fictional characters: two with incarceration experience and two without.
Narratives were randomized across sessions so that all five narratives per group were presented across the longitudinal follow-up.

Stimuli represented ethnic diversity, with character's ethnicity (Afro-descent or European descent) alternating across sessions so that all participants were exposed to both ethnic groups across the longitudinal assessment.

After the encoding phase, participants completed memory checks requiring them to match narratives with the corresponding faces to ensure they correctly remembered the identity of the characters (Fig. 2B).
To familiarize themselves with the structure of the task, participants completed twelve practice trials before the main experiment, using socially neutral character narratives and scenarios.

The absence of an overall group difference in social choices and the absence of a group-specific longitudinal FMθ change (Group × Session) in outgoing participants were not statistically equivalent to zero (TOST p > .05).
The longitudinal analyses in this group were therefore underpowered, and null effects among outgoing participants are consequently reported as inconclusive on the basis of equivalence tests.
To facilitate longitudinal follow-up, participants provided contact details on paper-based forms.
Participants still in prison were contacted through institutional channels, whereas released participants were contacted using the information provided at baseline.
Incoming participants were notified of upcoming follow-up sessions through letters sent via the prison communication system (Prison Cloud) or via institutional intermediaries.
At approximately 3 months post-release, participants were contacted to schedule follow-up assessments.
In contrast, for outgoing participants, all participants were sentenced and nearing release, making this distinction less relevant.

Exploratory D2 model comparisons indicated that social intentions among incoming participants were significantly associated with a broad set of individual characteristics, including education level (pFDR < .001), previous income (pFDR < .001), previous imprisonments (pFDR < .001), conviction status (pFDR < .001), sentence length (categorical: pFDR < .001; continuous: pFDR < .001), age (pFDR < .001), BAS score (pFDR < .001), psychiatricdisorder status (pFDR < .001), time spent in the current prison (pFDR < .001), drug use (pFDR < .001), BIS score (pFDR = .012), and previous employment (pFDR = .027).
Because participants were incarcerated individuals, access to potentially identifying data may be subject to ethical and dataprotection restrictions.
Participants were recruited across 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium, which varied in security level, regime, and capacity.

Participants were not originally excluded if they had a mental disorder, however those who experienced active psychosis during testing, who were transferred to a psychiatric unit, who were unable to complete the task, or who were non-compliant were excluded.

When release was delayed by up to six months beyond baseline, the second assessment was conducted while participants were still incarcerated (n=2), although this assessment was not included in the final analyses.
Most incoming participants were recruited from Brugge (31.0%), Jamioulx (20.7%), and Tournai (20.7%), followed by Nieuw Dendermonde (17.2%), Turnhout (6.9%), and Marche-en-Famenne (3.4%).

Outgoing participants were primarily recruited from Leuven Centraal (38.5%), while smaller proportions were recruited from Beveren (15.4%), Ittre (15.4%), and Leuze (15.4%), and few participants from Ruiselede Agricultural Correctional Facility (7.7%) and Saint-Hubert Detention Center (7.7%).
Age Incoming participants were significantly younger than outgoing participants.
Incoming participants had a mean age of 35.97 years (SD = 11.89), whereas outgoing participants had a mean age of 44.62 years (SD = 10.70).

A non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test revealed that outgoing participants had significantly longer sentence lengths than incoming participants (U = 69.0, p < .001), with median sentence length categories corresponding to 1-3 years for incoming participants and 5-10 years for outgoing participants.
For outgoing participants, PCQ variables were assessed while participants were still incarcerated at baseline and were therefore treated as baseline constants across sessions.

text.text: Social decision-making is central to successful reintegration following incarceration, yet whether imprisonment changes how people treat individuals with versus without a criminal history remains unclear.

In this preregistered longitudinal study, newly detained (incoming, n = 34) and newly released (outgoing, n = 13) individuals completed a social decision task with EEG at three sessions over eight months, choosing whether to direct prosocial or antisocial actions toward characters described as having an incarceration history (here termed incarceration-history targets) or not (community targets).
Frontal midline theta (FMθ) was recorded as an index of choice-related conflict.
Prison-climate and quality-of-life measures were also collected.

Across groups, participants identified more strongly with (formerly) incarcerated individuals, yet directed more antisocial intentions toward incarceration-history targets and more prosocial intentions toward community targets.
Incoming participants showed a reduction in prosocial community intentions after four months that rebounded by eight months.
Incoming participants showed higher FMθ than outgoing participants early in incarceration, with a progressive reduction over time in all groups, consistent with reduced decision conflict.
Exploratory analyses linked social intentions to prison-environment and well-being factors.

Because the target types differed in criminal history and, inevitably, in how positively they were described, these effects are best understood as responses to stigma linked with incarceration-history rather than to group membership.
These findings suggest that incarceration and release involve distinct adaptations in social decision-making toward (ex-)prisoners, with dissociable behavioural and neural markers.
Attitudes toward people with a criminal history are the social dimension most directly implicated in reintegration.

A criminal record marks a person as a member of a devalued category, attracting stigma that constrains access to housing, employment, and relationships and that (ex-)prisoners may internalise themselves (LeBel, 2008; Moore et al., 2016; Pager, 2003).
text.formatted: A criminal record marks a person as a member of a devalued category, attracting stigma that constrains access to housing, employment, and relationships and that (ex-)prisoners may internalise themselves <ref type="bibr">(LeBel, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Moore et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pager, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Reintegration therefore depends not only on how the community treats those who have offended, but on how incarcerated and recently released individuals themselves come to regard, approach, or avoid others who share, or do not share, that history (Abo et al., 2022; Keene et al., 2018; Visher & Travis, 2011).
text.formatted: Reintegration therefore depends not only on how the community treats those who have offended, but on how incarcerated and recently released individuals themselves come to regard, approach, or avoid others who share, or do not share, that history <ref type="bibr">(Abo et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Keene et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Visher & Travis, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the present study operationalises this social dimension as prosocial and antisocial intentions directed toward characters described as having a criminal history versus a conventional life, and asks whether incarceration and release shift these attitudes linked with incarceration-history.
Social identity offers one interpretive lens on such attitudes as well.

According to Social Identity Theory, part of the self-concept derives from group membership, and social categorization fosters preference for one's own group and, at times, prejudice toward others (Tajfel & Turner, 1986), reflecting a basic need to belong (Baumeister & Leary, 1995; Cacioppo & Patrick, 2008).
text.formatted: According to Social Identity Theory, part of the self-concept derives from group membership, and social categorization fosters preference for one's own group and, at times, prejudice toward others <ref type="bibr">(Tajfel & Turner, 1986)</ref>, reflecting a basic need to belong <ref type="bibr">(Baumeister & Leary, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cacioppo & Patrick, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Such tendencies may become particularly pronounced in environments characterized by exclusion, uncertainty, and social threat, such as incarceration.
As such, prisons represent a particularly relevant context for examining how social identities emerge, evolve, and shape interpersonal behaviour, with direct implications for reintegration.

Examining how incarcerated individuals orient prosocial and antisocial behaviour toward fellow incarcerated and non-incarcerated individuals may therefore provide important insights into the social adaptations associated with imprisonment and release.
Imprisonment is characterized by social exclusion (Aureli et al., 2020; Traversa et al., 2026), where prisoners are physically separated from society (Schliehe et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Imprisonment is characterized by social exclusion <ref type="bibr">(Aureli et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Traversa et al., 2026)</ref>, where prisoners are physically separated from society <ref type="bibr">(Schliehe et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As they are forced to cohabit with other prisoners under constrained and often overcrowded conditions (Schaefer et al., 2017), prisoners are progressively embedded within a closed social environment in which fellow prisoners may become one of the few sources of affiliation and social support (Traversa et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As they are forced to cohabit with other prisoners under constrained and often overcrowded conditions <ref type="bibr">(Schaefer et al., 2017)</ref>, prisoners are progressively embedded within a closed social environment in which fellow prisoners may become one of the few sources of affiliation and social support <ref type="bibr">(Traversa et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, incarceration may foster the development of a distinct prisoner identity, potentially strengthening identification with other incarcerated individuals while simultaneously increasing distance toward nonincarcerated individuals.

Therefore, an important scientific and societal challenge is to understand how incarceration shapes social identity and, in turn, influences prosocial and antisocial tendencies toward individuals with and without incarceration history.
Criminal Social Identity (CSI) applies SIT to offending and incarceration contexts (Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Criminal Social Identity (CSI) applies SIT to offending and incarceration contexts <ref type="bibr">(Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Previous work suggests that CSI is shaped by complex interactions between individual and environmental factors, including peer relationships, social exclusion, stigma, and prior experiences of rejection (Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Previous work suggests that CSI is shaped by complex interactions between individual and environmental factors, including peer relationships, social exclusion, stigma, and prior experiences of rejection <ref type="bibr">(Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these processes are unlikely to be static.
Rather, they may be dynamically influenced by the prison environment itself, particularly during critical transitions such as prison entry and release.
Despite growing interest in prisoner social identity and prosociality, important gaps remain in the literature.

First, most existing studies rely on self-report measures assessing identity, trust, stigma, or prosociality (Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013; Mosso et al., 2024; Traversa et al., 2026), while relatively few investigate actual social decision-making behaviour using ecological or incentivized paradigms (Birkeland et al., 2014; Chmura et al., 2017; Khadjavi & Lange, 2013).
text.formatted: First, most existing studies rely on self-report measures assessing identity, trust, stigma, or prosociality <ref type="bibr">(Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mosso et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Traversa et al., 2026)</ref>, while relatively few investigate actual social decision-making behaviour using ecological or incentivized paradigms <ref type="bibr">(Birkeland et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chmura et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Khadjavi & Lange, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Second, studies examining prosocial or antisocial tendencies in prisoners produced inconsistent findings.

Some studies found levels of altruism and cooperation comparable to non-incarcerated populations, both when prisoners interacted with other prisoners and with individuals from the general population (Birkeland et al., 2014; Chmura et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Some studies found levels of altruism and cooperation comparable to non-incarcerated populations, both when prisoners interacted with other prisoners and with individuals from the general population <ref type="bibr">(Birkeland et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chmura et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, other work reported reduced cooperation, trust, and reciprocity among offenders both when interacting with individuals outside the criminal justice system (Clark et al., 2015), or with incarcerated offenders (Scheeff et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In contrast, other work reported reduced cooperation, trust, and reciprocity among offenders both when interacting with individuals outside the criminal justice system <ref type="bibr">(Clark et al., 2015)</ref>, or with incarcerated offenders <ref type="bibr">(Scheeff et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, several studies suggest that prisoners may display increased prosociality under specific contextual conditions.

For example, incarcerated women showed higher cooperation rates with anonymous partners than students in Prisoner's Dilemma paradigms (Khadjavi & Lange, 2013), while organized crime members displayed particularly strong cooperation and loyalty compared to ordinary offenders and non-criminal controls (Nese et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For example, incarcerated women showed higher cooperation rates with anonymous partners than students in Prisoner's Dilemma paradigms <ref type="bibr">(Khadjavi & Lange, 2013)</ref>, while organized crime members displayed particularly strong cooperation and loyalty compared to ordinary offenders and non-criminal controls <ref type="bibr">(Nese et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, only a limited number of studies have explicitly examined the intergroup dimension of prisoner social behaviour.

Among these, Guo et al. (2020) reported evidence of ingroup favouritism, showing that prisoners exerted greater effort when helping individuals with a shared prisoner identity compared to individuals from outside the prison.
text.formatted: Among these, <ref type="bibr">Guo et al. (2020)</ref> reported evidence of ingroup favouritism, showing that prisoners exerted greater effort when helping individuals with a shared prisoner identity compared to individuals from outside the prison.

text.text: These inconsistencies may partly stem from the fact that most studies do not explicitly consider the intergroup context in which social decisions occur.
Specifically, little is known about whether incarceration shapes the distinction prisoners make between individuals with and without incarceration history.
Importantly, intergroup biases are expressed not only behaviourally but also neurally.

Research on intergroup empathy bias consistently shows reduced neural responses to outgroup relative to ingroup suffering (Amodio & Cikara, 2021; Vollberg & Cikara, 2018), and helping or empathizing with outgroup members appears to induce greater cognitive conflict than ingroup-directed behaviour (Amodio et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Research on intergroup empathy bias consistently shows reduced neural responses to outgroup relative to ingroup suffering <ref type="bibr">(Amodio & Cikara, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vollberg & Cikara, 2018)</ref>, and helping or empathizing with outgroup members appears to induce greater cognitive conflict than ingroup-directed behaviour <ref type="bibr">(Amodio et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Past electroencephalography (EEG) research has consistently shown that stronger cognitive conflict is associated with increased frontal midline theta (FMθ) activity (4-8 Hz), a neural marker implicated in conflict monitoring and cognitive control processes (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cohen & Cavanagh, 2011; Cohen, 2014; Nigbur et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Past electroencephalography <ref type="bibr">(EEG)</ref> research has consistently shown that stronger cognitive conflict is associated with increased frontal midline theta (FMθ) activity (4-8 Hz), a neural marker implicated in conflict monitoring and cognitive control processes <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh & Frank, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cohen & Cavanagh, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cohen, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nigbur et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Extending these findings to prosocial decision-making, Pech and Caspar (2024) showed that participants exhibited increased FMθ activity and longer reaction times during prosocial intentions toward outgroup compared to ingroup individuals, consistent with greater cognitive conflict when helping outgroup members.
text.formatted: Extending these findings to prosocial decision-making, <ref type="bibr">Pech and Caspar (2024)</ref> showed that participants exhibited increased FMθ activity and longer reaction times during prosocial intentions toward outgroup compared to ingroup individuals, consistent with greater cognitive conflict when helping outgroup members.

text.text: Related work further demonstrated reduced neural empathic responses toward outgroup pain and that it can be voluntarily modulated depending on motivational and contextual factors (Caspar et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Related work further demonstrated reduced neural empathic responses toward outgroup pain and that it can be voluntarily modulated depending on motivational and contextual factors <ref type="bibr">(Caspar et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This preregistered longitudinal study investigates how incarceration and release influence prosocial and antisocial intentions toward people with versus without a criminal history, and the neural activity associated with conflict and control demands during these choices.

Newly detained ("incoming") and newly released ("outgoing") individuals were followed over eight months at three sessions, to test whether these attitudes shift during early imprisonment and reintegration.

Participants performed a modified version of the intended-prosociality task (Pech & Caspar, 2024), directing prosocial and antisocial actions toward characters described as having a criminal history or a conventional life.
text.formatted: Participants performed a modified version of the intended-prosociality task <ref type="bibr">(Pech & Caspar, 2024)</ref>, directing prosocial and antisocial actions toward characters described as having a criminal history or a conventional life.

text.text: Neural activity was simultaneously recorded using EEG, with analyses focusing on FMθ activity.

The highly interdependent nature of prison life may promote solidarity and affiliation among incarcerated individuals, potentially strengthening identification with fellow prisoners and increasing prosocial intentions toward fellow prisoners and distance from the wider community (Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2020; Jetten et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The highly interdependent nature of prison life may promote solidarity and affiliation among incarcerated individuals, potentially strengthening identification with fellow prisoners and increasing prosocial intentions toward fellow prisoners and distance from the wider community <ref type="bibr">(Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Guo et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Jetten et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, prisoners may actively distance themselves from the prisoner identity because of its stigmatized and socially devalued nature (Mosso et al., 2024), and orient toward the community, especially after release, when stigma and disrupted relationships are common barriers (Keene et al., 2018; Visher & Travis, 2011), and a sense of belonging supports reintegration (Abo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Conversely, prisoners may actively distance themselves from the prisoner identity because of its stigmatized and socially devalued nature <ref type="bibr">(Mosso et al., 2024)</ref>, and orient toward the community, especially after release, when stigma and disrupted relationships are common barriers <ref type="bibr">(Keene et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Visher & Travis, 2011)</ref>, and a sense of belonging supports reintegration <ref type="bibr">(Abo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Given these competing theoretical possibilities, bidirectional hypotheses regarding the effects of incarceration and release were preregistered.
Importantly, individuals differ considerably in their pre-existing psychosocial characteristics, which can impact their experience of the prison environment (Liebling & Maruna, 2005).
text.formatted: Importantly, individuals differ considerably in their pre-existing psychosocial characteristics, which can impact their experience of the prison environment <ref type="bibr">(Liebling & Maruna, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Social tendencies may therefore also be associated with perceived prison climate and reintegration conditions.

To examine these factors, incarcerated participants completed the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ), assessing perceptions of autonomy, safety, relationships, and opportunities within prison (Bosma et al., 2020).
text.formatted: To examine these factors, incarcerated participants completed the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ), assessing perceptions of autonomy, safety, relationships, and opportunities within prison <ref type="bibr">(Bosma et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Perceptions of post-release conditions were evaluated with the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ), which captures dimensions related to quality of life, social integration, and access to meaningful resources after imprisonment (Harper et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Perceptions of post-release conditions were evaluated with the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ), which captures dimensions related to quality of life, social integration, and access to meaningful resources after imprisonment <ref type="bibr">(Harper et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Exploratory analyses investigated whether individual differences in individual and environmental factors were associated with longitudinal changes in social decision-making.
Overall, the current study aims to provide the first longitudinal investigation of how incarceration shapes prosocial and antisocial behaviour at both behavioural and neural levels.

Using experimental social neuroscience methods, the study examines whether imprisonment strengthens affiliation among prisoners and reinforces exclusion toward the general population, or instead produces more complex patterns of social adaptation.
Participants Three hundred and fifty (N = 350) male prisoners from 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium participated in the study.
Only men were recruited to the prisoner groups.
Women make up roughly 4% of the Belgian prison population (World Prison Brief, 2024) and are held in only a small number of establishments.
text.formatted: Women make up roughly 4% of the Belgian prison population <ref type="bibr">(World Prison Brief, 2024)</ref> and are held in only a small number of establishments.

text.text: Therefore, recruiting women would have introduced bias on gender, and their concentration in a few prisons would have confounded gender with prison site.
The prisoner groups were therefore restricted to men.
The study protocol was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) on August 10, 2023 (DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/M4TS9).
text.formatted: The study protocol was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) on August 10, 2023 (DOI: <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/M4TS9">10.17605/OSF.IO/M4TS9</ref>).

text.text: Power analyses with G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) for the Group (2level: Incoming/Outgoing) × Session (3-level) × Scenario (2-level: Pro-/Anti-Social) interactions, using a repeated-measures approximation, indicated a total target sample size of 28 participants (14 per group) to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25) with 95% power.
text.formatted: Power analyses with G*Power <ref type="bibr">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref> for the Group (2level: Incoming/Outgoing) × Session (3-level) × Scenario (2-level: Pro-/Anti-Social) interactions, using a repeated-measures approximation, indicated a total target sample size of 28 participants (14 per group) to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25) with 95% power.

text.text: However, G*Power misspecifies designs that combine between-and within-subject interactions(Brysbaert, 2019), and our confirmatory analyses used linear mixed-effects models (LMM).
Therefore, additional simulation-based power analyses were conducted for the actual model.
This analysis was not part of the preregistered plan and is reported as a deviation (see Supplementary S1).
To avoid circularity, the assumed effect size was fixed independently of the observed results.

Simulating the Group × Session × Scenario interaction on the binomial choice model (64 free-choice trials per scenario per session), and assuming a small interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) with moderate between-participant variability in the session change, 80% power was reached at approximately 30 participants per group.
Main effects and lower-order interactions required fewer participants.
Because longitudinal prison research entails high attrition, baseline recruitment targets were set substantially higher than these completing-sample targets.
Details on sample size estimation, recruitment and inclusion/exclusion criteria are provided in Supplementary S1.
Communication with prisoners was facilitated by prison staff to arrange appointments.
All eligible candidates received oral and written information and provided written informed consent.

For incarcerated participants, consent procedures were conducted without staff present to minimize perceived links with the judicial system, and participants were explicitly informed of the research team's independence from the penitentiary and judicial system.
Incoming and outgoing prisoners completed behavioural tasks with EEG recordings and questionnaires at each session and received financial compensation (€10 for questionnaires, €10 for tasks).
The study was part of a broader longitudinal project on executive functioning in incarceration, including multiple cognitive paradigms.
Incoming prisoners were assessed within four to seven weeks following incarceration (M = 31.4 days, SD = 13.9).
This recruitment window allowed the baseline to capture early-stage incarceration while ensuring sufficient stability in participants' status.
The outgoing group consisted of prisoners assessed shortly before release (M = 19.7 days before release, SD = 35.0).
To specifically examine the effects of prolonged incarceration, only participants who had been detained for at least six months prior to baseline were included.
On average, outgoing participants had spent 1,378 days in detention (SD = 1,411).
To facilitate follow-up, several retention strategies were employed (see Supplementary S2 for details, including attrition rates).
text.formatted: To facilitate follow-up, several retention strategies were employed (see Supplementary <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref> for details, including attrition rates).

text.text: The right to withdraw from the study at any given time without any consequences for the participants was emphasized.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ghent University (2023-085A).
Complete datasets with the three experimental sessions were collected for 34 incoming and 13 outgoing participants.
Mean S1-S2 retest intervals were 129.7 days (SD = 19.3) for incoming, and 139.7 days (SD = 23.7) for outgoing participants.
Mean S2-S3 retest intervals were 134.4 days (SD = 38.9) for incoming and 150.4 days (SD = 44.8) for outgoing participants.
For EEG analyses, participants with excessive noise or insufficient usable trials were excluded, resulting in final longitudinal EEG samples of 29 incoming and 11 outgoing participants.
Descriptive statistics for individual and incarceration-related variables are reported in Supplementary S4.
Incoming participants were significantly younger than outgoing participants (t = -2.34, p = .027).
Age was therefore included as a covariate in statistical analyses.

Education levels did not differ significantly between groups (p = .762) with the majority of both incoming and outgoing participants reporting secondary education (58.6% and 53.8%, respectively), whereas smaller proportions reported no formal education, primary education, or higher education.
Sentence-related characteristics differed significantly between groups.
Among incoming participants, 62.1% were convicted at baseline, whereas 37.9% were on remand or pre-trial detention.
Sentence lengths were significantly longer in outgoing compared to incoming participants (U = 69.0, p < .001).
text.formatted: Sentence lengths were significantly longer in outgoing compared to incoming participants (U = 69.0, p < .001).

text.text: Incoming participants were relatively evenly distributed across remand/pre-trial detention (37.9%), sentences of 1-3 years (20.7%), 3-5 years (20.7%), and 5-10 years (20.7%).
In contrast, outgoing participants were predominantly serving longer sentences, with 69.2% reporting sentence lengths of 5-10 years.
Incoming participants with sentences shorter than one year were intentionally excluded during recruitment in order to reduce attrition risk across longitudinal follow-ups.
Re-incarceration rates did not differ significantly between incoming and outgoing participants (U = 164.0, p = .498).
Among incoming participants, 31.0% reported only the current incarceration, whereas 27.6% reported two incarcerations and 41.4% reported three to five incarcerations.
Similarly, among outgoing participants, 30.8% reported only the current incarceration, 23.1% reported two incarcerations, and 46.2% reported three to five incarcerations.
Overall, repeated incarceration was common in both groups (incoming: 69.0%; outgoing: 69.2%).

This variable reflects participants' self-reported history of previous incarcerations and should not be interpreted as a measure of recidivism, for which rates can vary depending on the definition, follow-up period, and outcome considered.
Participants could report multiple offences, therefore percentages should be interpreted independently.
The most frequently reported types of offence in incoming participants were violent offences (27.6%), followed by drug-related, non-violent property and sexual offences (24.1% each).
Among outgoing participants, the most commonly reported were non-violent property and sexual offences (38.5% each), followed by drug-related (30.8%), life and violent offences (23.1% each).
Testing sessions within prisons were conducted in available rooms, including classrooms, consultation rooms, and activity spaces (Fig. 1).
