text.text: Follow-up sessions outside prison took place at participants' homes, social housing centers, workplaces, or rented testing spaces.
Each session lasted approximately two hours and included five cognitive tasks with EEG recordings (1-1.5 hours), followed by 30-60 minutes of questionnaires.
Tasks were administered on laptops using PsychoPy (Python 3.10).
Two laptops were used simultaneously during data collection (Lenovo ThinkBook 15 G3 ACL and Dell Latitude 5530; 15.6-inch screens; 1920×1080 resolution; 60 Hz refresh rate).
Responses were provided using a standard computer mouse to minimize head movements and facilitate participation for individuals with limited computer experience.
Task order was randomized across participants to reduce fatigue and order effects.
Questionnaires were completed on paper before or after the tasks depending on practical constraints and participant availability.
The Intended Pro-/Anti-Sociality Task was adapted from Pech and Caspar (2024) to investigate social decision-making towards individuals with and without incarceration history.

This task was designed to accommodate participants who were less familiar with computer use than the convenience samples typically recruited in psychological research, and was therefore specifically adapted to the present population.
During the encoding phase (Fig. 2A), participants were introduced to four fictional characters: two with incarceration experience and two without.
text.formatted: During the encoding phase (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>), participants were introduced to four fictional characters: two with incarceration experience and two without.

text.text: Participants read short narratives about each character and rated to which extent they identified with them on a 4-point scale ("No", "Not really", "Partly", "Yes").
Narratives were randomized across sessions so that all five narratives per group were presented across the longitudinal follow-up.

Stimuli represented ethnic diversity, with character's ethnicity (Afro-descent or European descent) alternating across sessions so that all participants were exposed to both ethnic groups across the longitudinal assessment.
Face stimuli were randomly selected from the Chicago Face Database (Ma et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Face stimuli were randomly selected from the Chicago Face Database <ref type="bibr">(Ma et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, the incarceration-history and community targets narratives differed not only in incarceration history but, inevitably, in valence.

Indeed, characters with incarceration experience were described through a criminal record, including an offence, sometimes along with a sentence, whereas characters without incarceration experience were described through a conventional life history.
This mirrors how incarceration-history information is encountered in everyday life.
However, it also means that target group status and the positivity of the descriptions are intertwined by design.
For clarity, the two target types with incarceration experience are referred to as incarceration-history characters and characters without such a history as community targets.
These labels denote the incarceration-history contrast between the targets throughout.

After the encoding phase, participants completed memory checks requiring them to match narratives with the corresponding faces to ensure they correctly remembered the identity of the characters (Fig. 2B).
text.formatted: After the encoding phase, participants completed memory checks requiring them to match narratives with the corresponding faces to ensure they correctly remembered the identity of the characters (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>).

text.text: Incorrect or omitted responses had to be repeated until correct.
Characters were reintroduced twice, following each break, to maintain familiarity throughout the task.
To familiarize themselves with the structure of the task, participants completed twelve practice trials before the main experiment, using socially neutral character narratives and scenarios.
The main task consisted of selecting toward which character an action should be directed (Fig. 2C).
text.formatted: The main task consisted of selecting toward which character an action should be directed (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2C</ref>).

text.text: Four prosocial (e.g.
"These two people have asked your help for moving.
Who are you helping move?") and four antisocial action scenarios (e.g.
"These two people are on the opposing team during a football game.

Who do you tackle, so that you hurt them and they cannot play?") were randomly sampled from a list of 16 scenarios and alternated across sessions so that all scenarios were eventually presented during the longitudinal study.
Each scenario was repeated twice across 16 blocks.
Scenarios were displayed for 10 seconds, accompanied by illustrative images and optional audio recordings to reduce cognitive load.
Examples of characters' narratives and scenarios are presented in Supplementary S3.
Each block contained 16 trials corresponding to all combinations of character pairings.
During each trial, participants chose between the two characters on screen by clicking on their name with the mouse.
After each trial, a fixation cross was displayed for 0.8-1.2 seconds and the mouse cursor was reset to the center of the screen to ensure sufficient time for EEG analyses.
Trials included free-choice conditions (incarceration-history vs. community target) and forced-choice conditions (same target presented twice).
The task included 128 free-choice trials and 128 forced-choice trials, for a total of 256 trials (~20 minutes).

Forced-choice trials were included to facilitate comparison of neural activity associated with decisions in pro-and antisocial contexts towards incarceration-history and community target, in case some participants never selected one character in some experimental conditions.
Who are you helping move?") and anti-social scenarios (e.g.
These two people are on the opposing team during a football game.
Who do you tackle, so that you hurt them and they cannot play?).
After reading one scenario, they were instructed to select the individual toward whom they would direct the action.

Trials included forcedchoice conditions, in which the same individual was presented twice, and free-choice conditions, in which participants chose between one incarceration-history or one community target.
Following each scenario presentation, a fixation cross was displayed for 800-1200 ms before the decision screen appeared.
Participants in each group completed a series of questionnaires examining prison and postrelease life conditions, well-being, and individual characteristics.
These measures were included as exploratory predictors of social decision-making at the behavioural and neural levels.
Perceptions of the prison environment were assessed using the validated Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ), administered at baseline in both cohorts and at follow-ups in incoming participants only.

The PCQ evaluates several dimensions of prison climate, including autonomy, safety, meaningful activities, contact with the outside, and relationships with staff and fellow prisoners (Bosma et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The PCQ evaluates several dimensions of prison climate, including autonomy, safety, meaningful activities, contact with the outside, and relationships with staff and fellow prisoners <ref type="bibr">(Bosma et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Participants also reported perceived detention severity and psychological distress using the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K6).

Outgoing participants reported post-release quality of life using the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ) at S2-S3 to evaluate five domains including inner peace, agency and energy, social connectedness, leisure, and spirituality (Harper et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Outgoing participants reported post-release quality of life using the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ) at S2-S3 to evaluate five domains including inner peace, agency and energy, social connectedness, leisure, and spirituality <ref type="bibr">(Harper et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Baseline assessments further included demographic and detention-related variables, while substance use and incarceration history were collected longitudinally.
Reward and punishment sensitivity were measured using the Behavioural Inhibition System/Behavioural Activation System (BIS/BAS) Scale (Carver & White, 1994).
text.formatted: Reward and punishment sensitivity were measured using the Behavioural Inhibition System/Behavioural Activation System (BIS/BAS) Scale <ref type="bibr">(Carver & White, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Additional methodological details are provided in Supplementary S5.
EEG was recorded using a 32-channel electrode cap with ActiveTwo system (BioSemi) system arranged according to the international 10-20 layout and sampled at 2048 Hz.
Preprocessing was performed in MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Preprocessing was performed in MNE-Python <ref type="bibr">(Gramfort et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The full procedure is detailed in Supplementary S6.
Prior to preprocessing, raw recordings were visually inspected to remove excessive noise.
Data were then processed using an automated pipeline.
Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was performed to remove ocular and muscular artifacts.
Components were classified automatically using ICLabel (Li et al., 2022; Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019) and only components labelled as "brain" or "other" with a probability ≥ .70 .
text.formatted: Components were classified automatically using ICLabel <ref type="bibr">(Li et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)</ref> and only components labelled as "brain" or "other" with a probability ≥ .70 .

text.text: Data were re-referenced offline using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST).
For time-frequency analyses, data were filtered between 1-40 Hz and segmented into response-locked epochs (-2 to 2 s relative to the keypress).
Trials containing artifacts were rejected using automated outlier detection.

Time-frequency representations (TFRs) were computed at the single-trial level and FMθ was subsequently extracted within a pre-response window (time: -1.0,-0.25 s ; frequency: 3-7Hz) identified from grand-average activity (Fig. 3) using a post-response baseline (0.0-1.0s).

text.text: Analyses focused on fronto-central channels (FC1, FC2, Fz, Cz), commonly associated with FMθ activity (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cohen, 2014).

TFR represents the average across all decision conditions, sessions, and participant groups.
Warmer colors indicate increased power relative to baseline, whereas cooler colors indicate decreased power.
The highlighted dashed red rectangle indicates the predefined FMθ window of interest (3-7 Hz; -1.0 to -0.25 s), selected based on grand-average activity across groups and sessions.
This window was used to extract trial-level FMθ power for statistical analyses.

The blue dashed rectangle illustrates the sensorimotor μ/β desynchronization window (approximately 8-25 Hz; -0.65 to 0.35 s), reflecting response preparation and motor execution processes associated with the button press.
This μ/β desynchronization is displayed for descriptive visualization only and was not included in the statistical analyses.
Baseline normalization was computed using the post-response interval from 0 to 1 s.
Insets illustrate the task structure, with the social decision phase (left) followed by the fixation period corresponding to the baseline window (right).

As a validation check of the task manipulation, character identification ratings were analysed using an LMM to verify whether participants identified more strongly with targets with or without incarceration history across sessions and groups, fit on the 47 participants with complete data at all three sessions (34 incoming, 13 outgoing).
The main behavioural outcome consisted of trial-level incarceration-history versus community target choices during free-choice trials.
Choices were analysed using a generalized LMM (GLMM) with a binomial link function.
Fixed effects included Group (incoming/outgoing), Session (S1-S3), Scenario Type (pro-/anti-social), and their interactions.
Decision times (DT) and mean-centred age were included as covariates.
Random effects included participant-level intercepts and slopes for within-subject factors Session and Scenario Type.
The model was fit on the same 47 participants (34 incoming and 13 outgoing).
The main neural outcome was trial-level FMθ amplitude during forced-choice trials.
FMθ was analysed using an LMM including fixed effects of Group, Session, Scenario Type, Target (incarceration-history/community), and their interactions, with DT and age included as covariates.
Random effects included participant-level intercepts and slopes for Session, Scenario Type, and Target.

Prior to modelling, trial-level FMθ values were screened for withinparticipant outliers, excluded when at least two of three criteria were met: an absolute zscore above 3, a deviation exceeding three median absolute deviations, or a value beyond 1.5 times the interquartile range.
To assess the robustness of the FMθ results to this exclusion, all neural models were also refit including outlier trials; these sensitivity analyses are reported in Supplementary S8.
Planned contrasts were examined using estimated marginal means (EMMs) with Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons.
The model was fit on the 40 participants with usable EEG at all three sessions (29 incoming and 11 outgoing).
Exploratory analyses examined the influence of questionnaire-derived individual and contextual predictors separately in incoming and outgoing participants.
Missing questionnaire and covariate data were handled using multiple imputation.

For outgoing participants, PCQ variables reflected baseline (pre-release) assessments, whereas GLQ variables from the first (S2) and second (S3) post-release assessments were evaluated as separate candidate predictors.

Candidate predictors were first tested individually into behavioural and neural mixed-effects models as interactions with the primary experimental factors (Session × Scenario for behavioural analyses; Session × Scenario × Target for neural analyses).
For each predictor, model fit was compared against the corresponding baseline model using pooled D2 tests across imputed datasets.
To account for multiple testing across predictors, false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied separately within each analysis.

For predictors surviving FDR correction, follow-up estimated marginal means and simple slope analyses were conducted to identify the specific Session × Scenario (and Session × Scenario × Target for FMθ) conditions driving the effects.

Because a non-significant result cannot by itself indicate the absence of an effect, the nonsignificant effects were additionally examined with equivalence tests (two one-sided tests) (Lakens, 2017; Lakens et al., 2018).

text.text: These tests were not part of the preregistered analysis plan and the equivalence bounds, procedure, and full results are provided in Supplementary S11.
Effects that were neither statistically significant nor statistically equivalent were interpreted as inconclusive.
Full details regarding models specifications, including imputation procedures and exploratory analyses are provided in Supplementary S7.

The main objective was to examine how incarceration and release shape prosocial and antisocial intentions directed toward people with versus without incarceration history, combining behavioural and neural markers.

Although both incoming and outgoing participants consistently identified more strongly with characters who had a criminal history than with community characters, this stronger identification did not translate into uniform behavioural favouritism toward them.
Instead, the results revealed a dissociation between subjective identification, social behaviour, and conflict-related neural activity.

Across groups and sessions, participants identified more strongly with incarcerated than nonincarcerated characters, and this pattern was already present shortly after incarceration in incoming participants and remained stable in outgoing participants after release (equivalence tests).
The design cannot establish whether this identification follows incarceration or precedes it, as individuals entering prison may already identify with marginalized or justiceinvolved groups.

CSI is thought to develop progressively through pre-existing peer affiliations and marginalization, with incarceration and prisonization potentially reinforcing and stabilizing it over time (Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013; Boduszek & Hyland, 2011; Walters, 2003).
text.formatted: CSI is thought to develop progressively through pre-existing peer affiliations and marginalization, with incarceration and prisonization potentially reinforcing and stabilizing it over time <ref type="bibr">(Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Boduszek & Hyland, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Walters, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Besides, criminalized populations often remain tied to these networks after release for material support, housing, and protection against isolation (Michel, 2024).
text.formatted: Besides, criminalized populations often remain tied to these networks after release for material support, housing, and protection against isolation <ref type="bibr">(Michel, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Identification with (formerly) incarcerated others may therefore reflect both pre-existing social positioning and subsequent adaptation to incarceration.
Importantly, this stronger identification did not translate into a behavioural preference for (formerly) incarcerated targets.

On the contrary, participants directed prosocial intentions toward community targets and antisocial intentions toward incarceration-history targets, so that behaviour tracked the valence of the targets' descriptions rather than the group with which participants more strongly identified.
A strict social-identity account would predict the opposite, namely an ingroup favouritism toward incarceration-history targets.
The observed pattern can be explained by a incarceration-history identity as ambivalent or stigmatized.

It could also be that, because target type was confounded with the valence of the descriptions, the effects observed reflect responses to the stigma attached to an incarceration history rather than to group membership per se.

The social-identity account is therefore one possible interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism (Balliet et al., 2014; Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013; Tajfel & Turner, 1986).
text.formatted: The social-identity account is therefore one possible interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism <ref type="bibr">(Balliet et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Boduszek, Adamson, Shevlin, Mallett, et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Tajfel & Turner, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Read through this lens, several features of the data are informative.
Identification did not entail unconditional solidarity with (formerly) incarcerated targets or hostility toward non-incarcerated others.

Rather, it appears an incarceration-history identity may be ambivalent, providing belonging while carrying stigma and social devaluation (Jetten et al., 2017; Mosso et al., 2024; Traversa et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Rather, it appears an incarceration-history identity may be ambivalent, providing belonging while carrying stigma and social devaluation <ref type="bibr">(Jetten et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mosso et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Traversa et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Higher antisocial intentions toward incarceration-history targets do not necessarily reflect hostility.
Instead, they may be perceived as less socially costly, reflecting expectations of reciprocity or tolerance among familiar others (Balliet et al., 2014; Imada et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Instead, they may be perceived as less socially costly, reflecting expectations of reciprocity or tolerance among familiar others <ref type="bibr">(Balliet et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Imada et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, several participants spontaneously reported assigning unpleasant actions to individuals "who would not mind", although anecdotal, it suggests perceived relational safety rather than dislike.
Such orientations are nonetheless highly context-dependent (Durrheim et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Such orientations are nonetheless highly context-dependent <ref type="bibr">(Durrheim et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Prison environments, marked by overcrowding, tension, and chronic stress (Beyens, 2019; Haney, 2001), may further shape these dynamics, as prolonged forced cohabitation can erode idealized solidarity and heighten interpersonal fatigue or distrust (Haney, 2006).
text.formatted: Prison environments, marked by overcrowding, tension, and chronic stress <ref type="bibr">(Beyens, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haney, 2001)</ref>, may further shape these dynamics, as prolonged forced cohabitation can erode idealized solidarity and heighten interpersonal fatigue or distrust <ref type="bibr">(Haney, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, testing by non-incarcerated researchers may have prompted identity management or socially desirable responding, including avoidance of overt alignment with a stigmatized "criminal" identity.
Whereas the behavioural findings were specific to the type of target and the valence of the scenario, the neural results operated at a general group level.

One reliable effect was a group difference as incoming participants showed higher FMθ amplitude than outgoing participants, across conditions and independent of whether the target had a criminal history.
Because this difference did not vary by scenario or target, it is unlikely to index the processing of incarceration-history stigma itself.
It more plausibly reflects the overall cognitive demand of the early-incarceration period.
Elevated FMθ is a well-established marker of conflict monitoring and cognitive control (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cohen, 2014).
text.formatted: Elevated FMθ is a well-established marker of conflict monitoring and cognitive control <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh & Frank, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cohen, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Its elevation early in incarceration is consistent with a state of heightened vigilance, uncertainty, and effortful regulation during initial adaptation to the prison environment.
This corresponds to the timewindow in which incoming participants also showed the most behavioural movement in how they oriented toward community targets.
From this perspective, the pattern is consistent with greater general cognitive engagement during early incarceration rather than target-specific conflict processing.
On the other hand, the valence-driven orientation toward specific targets is expressed behaviourally.
The smaller group difference observed near release would be consistent with a gradual settling of these adaptive demands.
However, because this is a between-groups comparison and the outgoing sample was underpowered, this interpretation remains speculative.
FMθ amplitude also declined across sessions overall, independent of group, scenario, or target.
However, because this effect did not survive the outlier-retention sensitivity analysis, it should be interpreted with caution.

If reliable, such a non-group-specific decline would more plausibly reflect a general reduction in cognitive engagement across repeated assessment, such as habituation or task familiarity, rather than an incarcerationspecific adaptation.
Exploratory analyses further suggested that social decision-making may be shaped by institutional experiences and individual characteristics.
These analyses are reported to generate rather than test hypotheses.

Among incoming participants, greater satisfaction with outside contacts and more positive staff-prisoner relationships were associated with more prosocial and fewer antisocial intentions toward community targets.

These associations align with evidence that maintaining connections with the outside world and supportive institutional relationships promote well-being, reduce institutionalization, and facilitate reintegration (Cochran, 2014; Liebling & Arnold, 2004).
text.formatted: These associations align with evidence that maintaining connections with the outside world and supportive institutional relationships promote well-being, reduce institutionalization, and facilitate reintegration <ref type="bibr">(Cochran, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Liebling & Arnold, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: One interpretation is that sustained contact with non-incarcerated others reduces the social distance and stigma attached to a incarceration-history label, fostering more positive orientations toward community targets (Allport, 1954; Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006).
text.formatted: One interpretation is that sustained contact with non-incarcerated others reduces the social distance and stigma attached to a incarceration-history label, fostering more positive orientations toward community targets <ref type="bibr">(Allport, 1954;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, greater availability of meaningful activities (at four months) and stronger prisoner-prisoner relationships were associated with fewer prosocial and more antisocial intentions toward community targets.

One valence-based interpretation is that deeper embedding in the prison social world makes incarcerationhistory descriptions more familiar and less negatively valenced, so that prosocial intent is extended more readily toward incarceration-history targets and, correspondingly, less toward community targets.

This is also one context in which a social-identity account fits well, as shared in-prison activities and peer bonds may reinforce identification with fellow (formerly) incarcerated individuals and a correspondingly sharper differentiation from community targets (Guo et al., 2020; Walters, 2003).
text.formatted: This is also one context in which a social-identity account fits well, as shared in-prison activities and peer bonds may reinforce identification with fellow (formerly) incarcerated individuals and a correspondingly sharper differentiation from community targets <ref type="bibr">(Guo et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Walters, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern was not uniform over time, however, as meaningful activities were associated with fewer antisocial intentions toward community targets at eight months, which may reflect the nature of some activities.

For instance skillsbased programmes or activities facilitated by non-incarcerated volunteers may increase contact with, and hence more positive orientations toward, the outside (Allport, 1954; Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006).
text.formatted: For instance skillsbased programmes or activities facilitated by non-incarcerated volunteers may increase contact with, and hence more positive orientations toward, the outside <ref type="bibr">(Allport, 1954;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Among outgoing participants, greater inner peace was associated with more prosocial intentions toward community targets over time, consistent with reintegration frameworks emphasizing the role of psychological well-being, meaning-making, and personal resources in social adaptation following release (Keene et al., 2018; Visher & Travis, 2011).
text.formatted: Among outgoing participants, greater inner peace was associated with more prosocial intentions toward community targets over time, consistent with reintegration frameworks emphasizing the role of psychological well-being, meaning-making, and personal resources in social adaptation following release <ref type="bibr">(Keene et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Visher & Travis, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: At the individual level, being diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder was associated, in both incoming and outgoing participants, with fewer prosocial intentions toward community targets, particularly early in incarceration and around release.
This is consistent with evidence linking psychiatric symptoms, particularly depressive symptoms, to social withdrawal and altered social cognition (Cruwys et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This is consistent with evidence linking psychiatric symptoms, particularly depressive symptoms, to social withdrawal and altered social cognition <ref type="bibr">(Cruwys et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the social-cure framework holds that identification with meaningful social groups can support health by providing belonging, support, and purpose (Haslam et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Accordingly, the social-cure framework holds that identification with meaningful social groups can support health by providing belonging, support, and purpose <ref type="bibr">(Haslam et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, incarcerated individuals with psychiatric difficulties may both struggle to maintain positive social relationships and, as a result, show reduced prosocial orientation toward community targets.
Higher reinforcement sensitivity was similarly associated with fewer prosocial intentions toward community targets.
Higher BAS scores among incoming participants at eight months and outgoing participants at baseline, and higher BIS scores among outgoing participants at four and eight months.

These associations fit evidence that social interactions engage reward-and punishment-processing systems, positive interactions can act as rewards (Baumeister & Leary, 1995; Krach et al., 2010), whereas social rejection or exclusion may be experienced as aversive (Dickinson & Dearing, 2014; Duffy et al., 2018).
text.formatted: These associations fit evidence that social interactions engage reward-and punishment-processing systems, positive interactions can act as rewards <ref type="bibr">(Baumeister & Leary, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Krach et al., 2010)</ref>, whereas social rejection or exclusion may be experienced as aversive <ref type="bibr">(Dickinson & Dearing, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Duffy et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, individual differences in reward and punishment sensitivity have been linked to variation in social motivation and functioning (Bijttebier et al., 2009; Gray, 1984).
text.formatted: Similarly, individual differences in reward and punishment sensitivity have been linked to variation in social motivation and functioning <ref type="bibr">(Bijttebier et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gray, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, altered reinforcement sensitivities may influence how individuals evaluate and engage with non-incarcerated others during incarceration and reintegration.
Among incoming participants, older age was the only predictor associated with higher FMθ amplitude.
Given the relatively young sample, this effect is unlikely to reflect age-related cognitive decline.

Instead, greater FMθ in relatively older prisoners may reflect increased recruitment of cognitive-control resources or more deliberate engagement during social decision-making (Zając-Lamparska et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Instead, greater FMθ in relatively older prisoners may reflect increased recruitment of cognitive-control resources or more deliberate engagement during social decision-making <ref type="bibr">(Zając-Lamparska et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation is consistent with work suggesting age-related changes in FMθ recruitment and flexibility during executive-control tasks (Darna et al., 2025; Depestele et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with work suggesting age-related changes in FMθ recruitment and flexibility during executive-control tasks <ref type="bibr">(Darna et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Depestele et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, older age was also associated with behaviour.
At baseline, older incoming participants showed fewer prosocial and more antisocial community target intentions.
This could reflect the number of incarcerations, as previous imprisonments showed an association with social intentions, although the post-hoc contrasts were not statistically significant.
Age may additionally index the accumulated duration of lived experience of social marginalization and stigma, which accumulates independently of the number of incarcerations.
Indeed, prolonged exposure to stigma and social exclusion has been linked to reduced trust and withdrawal from non-stigmatized groups (Keene et al., 2018; Link & Phelan, 2001).
text.formatted: Indeed, prolonged exposure to stigma and social exclusion has been linked to reduced trust and withdrawal from non-stigmatized groups <ref type="bibr">(Keene et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Link & Phelan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: A complementary social-identity reading is also well suited here.
Attitudes and social identities tend to become more stable and resistant to change with age (Krosnick & Alwin, 1989).
text.formatted: Attitudes and social identities tend to become more stable and resistant to change with age <ref type="bibr">(Krosnick & Alwin, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Although prosociality often increases with age it also becomes increasingly directed toward one's own group (Cutler et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Although prosociality often increases with age it also becomes increasingly directed toward one's own group <ref type="bibr">(Cutler et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Reduced prosocial and heightened antisocial orientation toward community targets in older prisoners may therefore reflect an age-related entrenchment of orientation toward incarcerationhistory targets rather than a general decline in prosociality.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the present findings.

Most importantly, the two target types were confounded since incarceration-history characters were described with a criminal record and community characters with a conventional life, so they differed in the valence of their descriptions as well as in incarceration-history status.
This has two consequences.
First, effects cannot be attributed to group membership itself.

Therefore they are interpreted primarily as responses to the incarceration-history descriptions and their associated stigma, and treat social-identity or intergroup-bias accounts as one possible interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

Conversely, because incarceration-history status and description valence covary, the present design cannot fully separate responses to the stigma of a criminal history specifically from responses to negatively valenced descriptions more generally.

Disentangling the two would require a design that orthogonalizes valence and incarceration-history status, for example, including negatively described community targets and positively described incarceration-history targets.

That participants nonetheless identified more strongly with incarceration-history characters indicates that this distinction was subjectively meaningful and not reducible to description valence alone.
Secondly, behavioural responses may have been influenced by social desirability or identity-management processes.
Testing was conducted individually in the presence of two researchers in the room, who may have been perceived as members of the non-incarcerated community.

Even though the experimenters were not keeping track of the participant's responses to avoid a social presence effect (Bond & Titus, 1983; McCambridge et al., 2014), it is possible that participants may have partly regulated their responses to avoid overt alignment with stigmatized "criminal" identities or antisocial attitudes.
text.formatted: Even though the experimenters were not keeping track of the participant's responses to avoid a social presence effect <ref type="bibr">(Bond & Titus, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McCambridge et al., 2014)</ref>, it is possible that participants may have partly regulated their responses to avoid overt alignment with stigmatized "criminal" identities or antisocial attitudes.

text.text: Third, the present task assessed hypothetical social intentions rather than real interpersonal behaviour.
Although the scenarios were designed to maximize ecological validity within prison settings, they inevitably simplify the complexity of real-world social interactions.
Prior work suggests that emotions such as guilt emerge after experiencing the emotional consequences of one's actions rather than during hypothetical situations (Andrade & Hoyle, 2022).
text.formatted: Prior work suggests that emotions such as guilt emerge after experiencing the emotional consequences of one's actions rather than during hypothetical situations (Andrade & Hoyle, 2022).

text.text: More immersive or ecologically realistic paradigms may therefore better capture prison interpersonal behaviour, but such approaches also raise important ethical challenges in incarcerated populations, particularly in specific antisocial or provocative situations.

Moreover, few experimental paradigms have attempted to examine prosocial and antisocial social decisions while preserving ecological realism in incarcerated populations, limiting the availability of validated task frameworks for comparison.

Future studies would benefit from combining experimental paradigms with qualitative approaches or immersive virtual social environments to better capture the contextual complexity of prison social cognition (Pan & Hamilton, 2018).
text.formatted: Future studies would benefit from combining experimental paradigms with qualitative approaches or immersive virtual social environments to better capture the contextual complexity of prison social cognition <ref type="bibr">(Pan & Hamilton, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, attrition was a substantial challenge, especially in the outgoing group (n = 13 at S3) which fell below both the preregistered target and the simulation-based estimate of approximately 30 participants per group.
The longitudinal analyses in this group were therefore underpowered, and null effects among outgoing participants are consequently reported as inconclusive on the basis of equivalence tests.
Voluntary participation may additionally have introduced selection bias.
Dropout nonetheless appeared to be driven primarily by practical follow-up constraints rather than disengagement from the study.

However, in outgoing participants, loss to follow-up after release may also reflect differences in post-release reintegration trajectories, including variability in housing stability, social functioning, or responsiveness to institutional contact.
As a result, participants retained at later follow-ups may not fully represent the broader population of released prisoners.

Because the prisoner groups were restricted to men by design, the present findings may not generalise to incarcerated women, whose experiences of incarceration-history stigma and reintegration trajectories may differ.

Despite these limitations, the present findings provide novel evidence that social adaptation during incarceration is not well captured by a simple strengthening of in-group preference toward (formerly) incarcerated others.
Instead, prosocial and antisocial intentions tracked the incarceration-history status and valence of the targets (Balliet et al., 2014; Turner et al., 1979).
text.formatted: Instead, prosocial and antisocial intentions tracked the incarceration-history status and valence of the targets <ref type="bibr">(Balliet et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Turner et al., 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Although both incoming and outgoing participants consistently identified more strongly with incarcerated individuals, the behavioural consequences of this identification appeared limited.

At the same time, antisocial decisions were more frequently directed toward individuals with incarceration history, highlighting that stronger prisoner identification does not necessarily translate into straightforward behavioural solidarity.
At the neural level, the early-incarceration period was marked by globally higher conflict-related activity in incoming than outgoing prisoners, without target-specific modulation.

The exploratory findings further suggest that social adaptation is shaped not only by how individuals relate to a incarcerationhistory identity, but also by prison experiences, especially in terms of social environment, and reintegration conditions.

Indeed, factors such as relationships with staff and fellow prisoners, contact with the outside world, psychological well-being, and psychiatric vulnerability were all associated with social decision-making, highlighting the importance of the broader social environment in shaping how (former) prisoners relate to both individuals with versus without an incarceration or a criminal history.
These findings may have important implications for reintegration.

Continued identification with incarcerated or formerly incarcerated individuals may influence social belonging, trust, and perceptions of stigma after release, while successful reintegration may depend in part on maintaining positive social connections and supportive environments both inside and outside prison.

Future research should therefore examine how reciprocal interactions between prisoners, former prisoners, and broader society contribute to social exclusion, stigma, and long-term reintegration outcomes.
To facilitate longitudinal follow-up, participants provided contact details on paper-based forms.
Comprehensive tracing details included participants' residential address, mobile phone number, email address, and social media profiles.
When possible, participants also provided contact details for alternative contacts (e.g., relatives, friends, social workers, or services they anticipated contacting upon release).

Similar strategies are commonly used in longitudinal studies involving marginalized or high-risk populations to ensure effective followup (Aitken et al., 2008; Stewart et al., 2021; Teague et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Similar strategies are commonly used in longitudinal studies involving marginalized or high-risk populations to ensure effective followup <ref type="bibr">(Aitken et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stewart et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Teague et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers ensured that participants understood how their secondary contacts' details would be used and that sensitive information, such as their criminal history, would not be disclosed to these individuals.
Several retention strategies were employed to maintain participant engagement throughout the follow-up period.
Participants still in prison were contacted through institutional channels, whereas released participants were contacted using the information provided at baseline.
When possible, participants transferred to another prison or re-incarcerated during follow-up were traced through the national penitentiary database (SIDIS) and reassessed in their new institution.
Participants could withdraw at any time without consequences.
Incoming participants were notified of upcoming follow-up sessions through letters sent via the prison communication system (Prison Cloud) or via institutional intermediaries.
This allowed participants who were employed within the prison to request time off or schedule testing outside of working hours.
During ongoing recruitment periods, participants eligible for follow-up were also contacted directly on recruitment days to confirm their continued interest and availability.

Participants transferred to a different penitentiary institution were identified through the SIDIS penitentiary database, and authorization to conduct testing in the new institution was obtained from the Belgian Federal Public Service Justice (Direction générale EPI -

For participants released from prison Participants who were scheduled for release within three weeks following baseline testing were asked to provide contact information, including a telephone number, email address, and/or residential address.
When available, contact details of a social worker, community center, or health service were also recorded.
At approximately 3 months post-release, participants were contacted to schedule follow-up assessments.
If initial contact attempts were unsuccessful, up to three follow-up messages were sent.
For participants who could not be reached through the provided contact information, secondary contacts were used to obtain updated contact details when available.
Letters were also sent to participants' last known residential address.
Participants who were re-incarcerated during the follow-up period were identified through the SIDIS database, provided they had consented to this monitoring in the informed consent procedure.
Participants who were re-incarcerated before S2 were excluded from follow-up analyses, whereas those re-incarcerated between S2 and S3 remained eligible for the final assessment.

For both incarcerated and released participants, they were considered lost to follow-up if they cancelled or were absent from two consecutive scheduled appointments, or did not respond to contact attempts for three consecutive weeks.
However, participants who contacted the research team within six months after release were allowed to re-enter the study if participation remained feasible.
Detailed participation rates and attrition at each follow-up wave are reported in Supplementary Figures S2-1 and S2-2.

Outgoing retention (bottom row) was 15.8% at S2 (of 133 participants at S1) and 61.9% at S3 (of 21 at S2).

text.text: All items were rated on a 6-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree;2 = Disagree;3 = Somewhat disagree;4 = Somewhat agree;5 = Agree;6 = Strongly agree).

Because the GLQ assesses post-release quality of life, it was administered only after release.
Consequently, GLQ predictors were included only in the exploratory analyses of the outgoing sample.

Scores obtained at the first (S2) and second (S3) post-release assessments were entered as separate candidate predictors, allowing the influence of quality of life at each follow-up to be examined independently.

Additional Predictors In addition to environmental perceptions, a set of candidate predictors was included covering demographic, incarceration-related, health, and psychological characteristics.

Demographic predictors included age (continuous), education level (ordinal), previous employment status (binary: yes/no), and self-reported income prior to incarceration (continuous; incoming sample only).
For outgoing participants, employment status following release was included as separate binary indicators for the first (S2) and second (S3) postrelease assessments.

Incarceration-related predictors were assessed at baseline only and included the number of previous imprisonments (continuous), time spent in the current prison (continuous), and sentence length (continuous).
For incoming participants, conviction status (convicted vs. pretrial detention) was additionally included.
Prison site was excluded from these analyses.

Because participant numbers varied substantially across establishments and prisons could not be meaningfully recoded into broader regime categories, site-level comparisons were not interpretable and are not reported.
In the incoming sample, sentence length at baseline was initially operationalized both as a continuous variable and a categorical factor.
The categorical representation allowed differentiation of participants on remand and those already convicted, capturing meaningful differences in legal status in this group.
In contrast, for outgoing participants, all participants were sentenced and nearing release, making this distinction less relevant.
Consequently, sentence length was modelled as a continuous variable in all outgoing analyses.
Substance use was operationalized as a binary variable reflecting any reported use of illicit substances within the past three months.
Psychiatric disorder status was similarly coded as a binary indicator (presence vs. absence of any diagnosed disorder).
The Behavioural Inhibition System (BIS) and Behavioural Activation System (BAS) scales (Carver & White, 1994) were used to assess individual differences in sensitivity to punishment  S5-4.
text.formatted: The Behavioural Inhibition System (BIS) and Behavioural Activation System (BAS) scales <ref type="bibr">(Carver & White, 1994)</ref> were used to assess individual differences in sensitivity to punishment  <ref type="table">S5</ref>-4.

text.text: The BAS scale comprises three subcomponents, including Drive, which measures goal pursuit, Fun Seeking, which measures novelty-seeking and impulsivity, and Reward Responsiveness.
All items were rated on a 4-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree;2 = Disagree;3 = Agree;4 = Strongly agree).
Scores were computed by summing items within each main scale (BIS/BAS).
Reverse-coded items were recoded prior to score computation.

EEG was recorded during task performance using a 32-electrode BioSemi ActiveTwo system (see http://www.biosemi.com/ for hardware details), positioned according to the international 10-20 system and sampled at 2048 Hz.
text.formatted: EEG was recorded during task performance using a 32-electrode BioSemi ActiveTwo system (see <ref type="url" target="http://www.biosemi.com/">http://www.biosemi.com</ref> for hardware details), positioned according to the international 10-20 system and sampled at 2048 Hz.

text.text: Two additional external electrodes were used to record mastoid activity.
Raw EEG data were acquired with ActiveView Software and converted to BIDS format.
Continuous data were resampled from 2048 to 512 Hz.
Preprocessing was conducted in MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013) using an automated pipeline.
text.formatted: Preprocessing was conducted in MNE-Python <ref type="bibr">(Gramfort et al., 2013)</ref> using an automated pipeline.

text.text: Prior to preprocessing, raw recordings were visually inspected to verify data quality and identify, visually and from prior records, bad channels.
For ICA decomposition, a separate copy of the continuous data was band-pass filtered between 1 and 30 Hz using an infinite impulse response (IIR) filter.
Power line noise was removed using notch filters at 50 Hz and its harmonics (up to 250 Hz).
ICA was computed using the Picard algorithm on EEG channels excluding bad channels.
Components were then automatically classified using the ICLabel classifier (Li et al., 2022; Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Components were then automatically classified using the ICLabel classifier <ref type="bibr">(Li et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Only components labelled as "brain" or "other" with a classification probability ≥ .70 were retained, all remaining components were removed.

Bad channels were interpolated using spherical spline interpolation, and data re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST), implemented through a spherical head model and forward solution (Gramfort et al., 2013; Yao, 2001; D. Yao et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Bad channels were interpolated using spherical spline interpolation, and data re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST), implemented through a spherical head model and forward solution <ref type="bibr">(Gramfort et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yao, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">D. Yao et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Data were band-pass filtered between 1 and 40 Hz and segmented into response-locked epochs (-2 to 2s).
Analyses focused on frontocentral electrodes (FC1, FC2, Fz, Cz), which are commonly associated with frontal midline theta activity (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cohen, 2014).
text.formatted: Analyses focused on frontocentral electrodes (FC1, FC2, Fz, Cz), which are commonly associated with frontal midline theta activity <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh & Frank, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cohen, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Epochs containing artifacts were excluded using a fully automated procedure applied to frontocentral electrodes (FC1, FC2, Fz, Cz) within a -1.5 to 1 s window surrounding the response.
Artifact detection was based on three signal properties: peak-to-peak amplitude, mean activity, and signal slope.
For each participant and electrode, trials exceeding an interquartile range (IQR)-based threshold (±2 × IQR) on any metric were automatically identified as outliers and removed from further analyses.
Across S1 to S3, trial rejection was 9.10% across incoming and outgoing participants included in the longitudinal EEG sample (IN: M = 8.77%, SD = 1.72; OUT: M = 9.84%, SD = 2.07).

Time-frequency representations (TFRs) were computed at the single-trial level using Morlet wavelets with frequencies ranging from 2 to 30 Hz (80 logarithmically spaced frequency bins) and logarithmically spaced cycles (4-14).
Power estimates were z-score normalized relative to a post-response baseline window (0.0-1.0 s post-response).
Trial-level theta estimates were extracted from frontocentral electrodes (FC1, FC2, Fz, Cz) within a time-frequency window identified from grand-average plots across all groups and sessions.
Specifically, theta activity was quantified within the 3-7 Hz and -1.0 to -0.250 s pre-response window for subsequent statistical analyses.
Participants contributing fewer than 10 valid trials per condition or fewer than 30 valid trials overall were excluded from EEG analyses.

text.text: This procedure removed 504 forced-choice trials (4.84% of eligible trials).
Model diagnostics were assessed for all mixed-effects models.
Convergence was evaluated using optimizer convergence codes and gradient-based diagnostics implemented in the lme4 package.
Random-effects structures were specified maximally when supported by the data and retained when models showed acceptable convergence and stable parameter estimates.
For LMM, residual distributions and fitted values were visually inspected to assess homoscedasticity and approximate normality.
Singular fits were additionally evaluated using variance estimates.
EMMs and planned contrasts were computed using the emmeans package to examine differences across sessions, groups, scenarios, and targets.
Tukey correction was applied for multiple comparisons.
Because the maximal random-effects structure (by-participant intercepts and random slopes for Session, Scenario, and Target) produced a singular fit, the structure was simplified.
The reported model retained by-participant intercepts and an uncorrelated random slope for Session, the within-subject factor of primary longitudinal interest.

This fit converged at a boundary estimate but preserves participant-level degrees of freedom for the within-subject Session effect, and is preferred over a simpler random-intercept-only model (Barr et al., 2013; Matuschek et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This fit converged at a boundary estimate but preserves participant-level degrees of freedom for the within-subject Session effect, and is preferred over a simpler random-intercept-only model <ref type="bibr">(Barr et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Matuschek et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The pattern of significant effects was unchanged across randomeffects structures as Group (F(1, 41.3) = 6.54, p = .014), Session (F(2, 54.1) = 4.59, p = .015), and age (F(1, 42.9) = 27.36, p < .001) remained significant, and no interaction reached significance.

text.text: Additional control analyses examined the potential influence of task order and ethnicity by adding each variable separately as a fixed-effect covariate using the same model structure.
These two variables were not significantly associated with the behavioural and neural outcomes, therefore they were not taken into account in the final analyses.

Exploratory analyses were conducted separately for incoming and outgoing participants to examine whether individual characteristics, prison-climate variables, and post-release quality-of-life measures were associated with social decision-making and FMθ activity.

Candidate predictors included demographic characteristics, incarceration-related variables, BIS/BAS scores, Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ) dimensions, and Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ) dimensions.
Missing questionnaire and covariate data were handled using multiple imputation (see below).

For outgoing participants, prison-climate variables reflected baseline (pre-release) assessments, whereas Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ) variables from the first (S2) and second (S3) post-release assessments were evaluated as separate candidate predictors.
For each predictor, a separate mixed-effects model was fitted across 20 imputed datasets.
For behavioural analyses, predictors were entered as interactions with Session and Scenario:
For neural analyses, predictors were entered as interactions with Session, Scenario, and Target:
Each predictor model was compared against the corresponding baseline model using D2 model-comparison tests pooled across imputations (Grund et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Each predictor model was compared against the corresponding baseline model using D2 model-comparison tests pooled across imputations <ref type="bibr">(Grund et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The D2 statistic evaluates whether inclusion of a predictor significantly improves model fit while accounting for uncertainty introduced by multiple imputation.
To control for multiple testing across predictors, p-values from D2 model comparisons were adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) procedure separately for each analysis.
Predictors surviving FDR correction were subsequently examined using post-hoc estimated marginal means (EMMs).

For continuous predictors, simple slopes were estimated within each Session × Scenario condition (and within each Session × Scenario × Target condition for FMθ analyses) using the emtrends() function.
For categorical predictors, pairwise EMM contrasts were computed using the emmeans package.
Only simple slopes (continuous predictors) and factor contrasts (categorical predictors) were interpreted and reported.
False discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied across the reported post-hoc tests within each analysis.
Estimates were pooled across imputations using Rubin's rules (Rubin, 1978).
text.formatted: Estimates were pooled across imputations using Rubin's rules <ref type="bibr">(Rubin, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: As for the confirmatory analyses, the exploratory predictor analyses were conducted on the outlier-removed sample.

A sensitivity analysis including all trials yielded a highly similar pattern of results with the same predictors surviving FDR correction, so the outlier-removed version is reported here for consistency with the main analyses.
Missing questionnaire and covariate data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) implemented with the mice package in R (Van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011).
text.formatted: Missing questionnaire and covariate data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) implemented with the mice package in R <ref type="bibr">(Van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Imputation was performed using the futuremice function to allow parallel computation.
Overall, missingness was low (1.83% on average for incoming participants and 2.52% for outgoing participants).
Higher missingness proportions (up to ~40%) were observed for a limited number of variables, mainly reflecting sparse or rare categories (e.g., specific medication or substance-use indicators).
For the incoming prisoner sample, 150 imputed datasets were generated, whereas 100 imputed datasets were generated for the outgoing prisoner sample, reflecting the smaller sample size.
Imputed datasets were generated with 400 iterations per imputation chain to ensure stable convergence of the algorithm.
The imputation model used predictive mean matching (PMM) as the primary imputation method (White et al., 2011).
text.formatted: The imputation model used predictive mean matching (PMM) as the primary imputation method <ref type="bibr">(White et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: For the statistical analyses reported in the manuscript, 20 imputed datasets were retained and pooled using Rubin's rule (D. B. Rubin, 2018).
The imputation model used a custom predictor matrix to specify which variables could be used to predict missing values.
This allowed to remove collinear and constant variables from the imputation model.
In addition, a masking rule was used to restrict imputation to testing sessions which were actually completed.
For a small number of variables that were constant (e.g., rare drug-use categories or offence types), imputation using the mice algorithm was not feasible.
In these cases, deterministic imputation using either the mean or the mode was applied to allow construction of composite indicators (e.g., binary indicators).
Participants with missing questionnaires in early sessions, but observed data at later sessions, were included in the imputation procedure.
Missingness in these cases primarily reflected procedural factors (e.g., questionnaires not returned or lost) rather than participant refusal.
On the other hand, participants who withdrew from the study or became ineligible for followup were not imputed forward.
One incoming participant, whose baseline and follow-up questionnaires were lost in transit (sent by post), could not be imputed.
This participant is therefore excluded from all questionnaire-based analyses (descriptive summaries and covariate/exploratory models), was retained in analyses requiring only task data.
To assess robustness, the FMθ model was refit on the full dataset including all trials.
Under this sample the random-effects structure retained by-participant intercepts and a Session slope (non-singular).

The main effect of Group remained, with incoming participants showing higher FMθ amplitude than outgoing participants (F(1, 40.2) = 5.09, p = .030), as did the positive association with age (F(1, 39.9) = 20.68, p < .001).
text.formatted: The main effect of Group remained, with incoming participants showing higher FMθ amplitude than outgoing participants (F(1, 40.2) = 5.09, p = .030), as did the positive association with age (F(1, 39.9) = 20.68, p < .001).

text.text: The main effect of Session, by contrast, was reduced to non-significance (F(2, 40.1) = 2.87, p = .068), indicating that the session-related decline observed in the primary analysis was not robust to outlier retention.
Decision time reached significance under this specification (F(1, 6797.5) = 5.20, p = .023), although it was non-significant in the primary model.
No other main effect or interaction was significant.
The Group and age effects are therefore robust to outlier handling, whereas the Session and decision-time effects are not and are interpreted with caution.
Exploratory predictor analyses were conducted separately for incoming and outgoing participants.
All p-values are false-discovery-rate (FDR) corrected over the full predictors set.
The behavioural-task and questionnaire samples are not identical.
Seven participants across the prisoner cohorts had usable task data but no questionnaire record.
Exploratory analyses are therefore run on the overlapping subset, which is smaller than either sample alone.

The preregistered sample-size target was derived from an a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) (medium effect, f = .25, 95% power).

text.text: Because G*Power approximates such designs as repeatedmeasures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions combining between-and within-subject factors (Brysbaert, 2019), and because the confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models, an additional simulation-based power analysis was conducted for the design actually used.
text.formatted: Because G*Power approximates such designs as repeatedmeasures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions combining between-and within-subject factors <ref type="bibr">(Brysbaert, 2019)</ref>, and because the confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models, an additional simulation-based power analysis was conducted for the design actually used.

text.text: This analysis was not preregistered and was performed after data collection.
To avoid circularity, the effect size was set by convention rather than from the observed estimates.

For each candidate sample size, datasets from a binomial GLMM were simulated with the full Group × Session × Scenario structure, a by-participant random intercept and random slopes for Session and Scenario, and 64 free-choice trials per scenario per session (aggregated to binomial counts within each participant × session × scenario cell).
The three-way Group × Session × Scenario interaction was tested with a likelihood-ratio test comparing the full model against a model retaining all two-way interactions.
Power was the proportion of 500 simulated datasets in which the interaction was detected at α = .05.

Assuming a small interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) and moderate between-participant variability in the session change (random-slope SD = 0.4 on the logit scale), 80% power for the threeway interaction was reached at approximately 30 participants per group in the present longitudinal design (two groups × three sessions).
Main effects and lower-order interactions reached 80% power at smaller samples.

The achieved longitudinal samples met the requirement for incoming participants (n = 34 with complete behavioural data; n = 29 with usable EEG across all three sessions) but fell below it for outgoing participants (n = 13 and n = 11, respectively); accordingly, null effects in the outgoing group are interpreted using equivalence tests as inconclusive rather than as evidence of absence (see Results).
Recruitment and Eligibility Criteria.
Participants were recruited across 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium, which varied in security level, regime, and capacity.
Eligibility for the study was restricted to individuals who had sufficient understanding of Dutch, French, or English and did not experience visual or motor impairments.
Participants who exhibited inappropriate behaviour towards the researchers were excluded, and in rare cases, prison staff denied participation for security or disciplinary reasons.
If they had already been approached by the researchers during a prior incarceration period, those candidates were excluded.

Participants were not originally excluded if they had a mental disorder, however those who experienced active psychosis during testing, who were transferred to a psychiatric unit, who were unable to complete the task, or who were non-compliant were excluded.
Additional eligibility criteria for the incoming group included transient incarceration, such as cases involving imminent release, extradition, or deportation.

For outgoing participants, eligibility was determined based on end-of-sentence dates and anticipated parole release, in consultation with prison staff, to ensure that follow-up assessments could be conducted after release.

When release was delayed by up to six months beyond baseline, the second assessment was conducted while participants were still incarcerated (n=2), although this assessment was not included in the final analyses.
Participants who were released more than six months after baseline were excluded from the cohort.

To capture the potential effects of prolonged incarceration on cognitive and social processes, only outgoing participants who had been incarcerated for a minimum of six months prior to release were included in the final sample.
Individuals released under limited detention regimes were excluded because this status simultaneously involves elements of incarceration and community reintegration.

Recruitment timelines, and prison specifications are detailed in Supplementary Table S1-1. Timelines differed across institutions due to logistical and administrative constraints, particularly related to prison overcrowding and repeated disruptions in prison access.

text.text: Data collection was notably interrupted in April 2024 following prolonged nationwide prison strikes, and access to several institutions remained intermittently restricted during the rest of the recruitment period.
The prison distribution at recruitment of participants completing all three sessions (S1-S2- S3) is shown in Supplementary Figure S1-1.

text.text: Most incoming participants were recruited from Brugge (31.0%), Jamioulx (20.7%), and Tournai (20.7%), followed by Nieuw Dendermonde (17.2%), Turnhout (6.9%), and Marche-en-Famenne (3.4%).

Outgoing participants were primarily recruited from Leuven Centraal (38.5%), while smaller proportions were recruited from Beveren (15.4%), Ittre (15.4%), and Leuze (15.4%), and few participants from Ruiselede Agricultural Correctional Facility (7.7%) and Saint-Hubert Detention Center (7.7%).

Several establishments include multiple internal regimes (e.g., closed, semiopen), and incarcerated individuals may transition between regimes depending on sentence stage, behaviour, and security classification.
Age Incoming participants were significantly younger than outgoing participants.
Incoming participants had a mean age of 35.97 years (SD = 11.89), whereas outgoing participants had a mean age of 44.62 years (SD = 10.70).
An independent-samples t-test revealed a significant group difference (t = -2.34, p = .027).
Therefore, age is included as a covariate in all the confirmatory analyses.
A non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test indicated no significant difference between incoming and outgoing participants (p = .762).
Overall, both groups were predominantly characterised by secondary-level education (Supplementary Figure S4-1).

All statistical tests were two-tailed.
Among incoming participants, 62.1% were convicted at baseline (n = 18) , whereas 37.9% were on remand or pre-trial detention (n = 11).
Sentence length differed significantly between incoming and outgoing participants (Supplementary Figure S4-2).

text.text: A non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test revealed that outgoing participants had significantly longer sentence lengths than incoming participants (U = 69.0, p < .001), with median sentence length categories corresponding to 1-3 years for incoming participants and 5-10 years for outgoing participants.

text.text: Importantly, prisoners who had already been convicted and received sentences shorter than one year were excluded during recruitment in order to minimise the likelihood of attrition across follow-up assessments.
Consequently, participants with sentences below one year were underrepresented in the incoming prisoner sample.

text.text: Sentence length categories were based on self-reported baseline information, and percentages were calculated relative to the total number of participants within each group.
These sentence durations should be interpreted cautiously, as they may not necessarily correspond directly to offence severity (e.g. in the case of repeated offences or cumulative sentencing).

In addition, sentence information was selfreported, hence it may not fully correspond to official judicial records, and, for the incoming group, it may not yet reflect the final judicial sentence at the time of assessment.
All statistical tests were two-tailed.
The number of incarcerations did not differ significantly between incoming and outgoing participants, as indicated by a non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test (U = 164.0, p = .498).
Repeated incarceration was common in both groups (Supplementary Figure S4-3).

text.text: Offence categories were derived from self-reported baseline information and were not mutually exclusive, since participants could be incarcerated for multiple offence types.

Among incoming participants, the most frequently reported offence categories were violent offences (27.6%), drug-related offences (24.1%), non-violent property offences (24.1%), and sexual offences (24.1%).
Smaller proportions of participants reported life offences (10.3%), violent property offences (10.3%), and offences related to arms possession, culpable negligence, or traffic offences (each 3.4%).

Among outgoing participants, the most commonly reported offence categories were non-violent property offences (38.5%) and sexual offences (38.5%), followed by drug-related offences (30.8%), life offences (23.1%), and violent offences (23.1%).
Arms-related and traffic offences were each reported by 15.4% of outgoing participants, while violent property offences were reported by 7.7% of the sample (Supplementary Figure S4-4).

For outgoing participants, PCQ variables were assessed while participants were still incarcerated at baseline and were therefore treated as baseline constants across sessions.

Preregistration)
The preregistered analysis plan did not include a procedure for quantifying evidence for the null.
A non-significant result cannot distinguish a genuine absence of effect from insufficient statistical power.

Thus, equivalence tests were conducted using the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure (Lakens, 2017; Lakens et al., 2018) for the three non-significant effects, including (i) the stability of identification with incarceration-history targets across sessions, (ii) the absence of overall group (incoming vs. outgoing) differences in social intentions, and (iii) the absence of longitudinal FMθ change in outgoing participants.
text.formatted: Thus, equivalence tests were conducted using the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure <ref type="bibr">(Lakens, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lakens et al., 2018)</ref> for the three non-significant effects, including (i) the stability of identification with incarceration-history targets across sessions, (ii) the absence of overall group (incoming vs. outgoing) differences in social intentions, and (iii) the absence of longitudinal FMθ change in outgoing participants.

text.text: Because these analyses were not preregistered, they are exploratory.
As no equivalence bounds were preregistered, smallest effects of interest (SESOI) were defined based on measurements rather than a priori.

Namely, it corresponds to half a point on the 4-point response scale (±0.5 points) for identification ratings, an odds ratio of 1.5 for social intentions on the log-odds scale (±log(1.5)), and a small effect in z-scored power of ±0.2 z for FMθ amplitude.

Following Lakens et al. (2018), an effect was considered statistically equivalent to zero when both one-sided tests were significant at α = .05, equivalently when its 90% confidence interval fell entirely within the equivalence bounds.
Effects that were neither statistically significant nor statistically equivalent were interpreted as inconclusive rather than as evidence for the null.
Because the chosen SESOIs are necessarily somewhat arbitrary, they should be treated as reasonable reference values rather than definitive thresholds.

Greater availability of meaningful activities was associated with fewer prosocial community target intentions at S2 (OR = 0.45, 95%CI [0.31, 0.64], pFDR < .001), along with more antisocial community target intentions at S2 (OR = 1.64, 95%CI [1.16, 2.34], pFDR = .047).
text.formatted: Greater availability of meaningful activities was associated with fewer prosocial community target intentions at S2 (OR = 0.45, 95%CI [0.31, 0.64], pFDR < .001), along with more antisocial community target intentions at S2 (OR = 1.64, 95%CI [1.16, 2.34], pFDR = .047).

text.text: At S3, greater availability of meaningful activities was instead associated with fewer antisocial community target intentions (OR = 0.71, 95%CI [0.57, 0.89], pFDR = .031).

Greater satisfaction with outside contacts was associated with more prosocial (OR = 2.02 [1.56, 2.60], pFDR < .001) and fewer antisocial (OR = 0.66, 95%CI [0.51, 0.84], pFDR = .011) community target intentions at S3.
text.formatted: Greater satisfaction with outside contacts was associated with more prosocial (OR = 2.02 [1.56, 2.60], pFDR < .001) and fewer antisocial (OR = 0.66, 95%CI [0.51, 0.84], pFDR = .011) community target intentions at S3.

text.text: Better prisoner-prisoner relationships were associated with fewer prosocial community target intentions at S1 (OR = 0.45, 95%CI [0.31, 0.63], pFDR < .001) but more antisocial community target intentions at S3 (OR = 2.21, 95%CI [1.55, 3.15], pFDR < .001).
text.formatted: Better prisoner-prisoner relationships were associated with fewer prosocial community target intentions at S1 (OR = 0.45, 95%CI [0.31, 0.63], pFDR < .001) but more antisocial community target intentions at S3 (OR = 2.21, 95%CI [1.55, 3.15], pFDR < .001).

text.text: Better staff-prisoner relationships were associated with more prosocial (OR = 1.50, 95%CI [1.14, 1.97], pFDR = .037) and fewer antisocial (OR = 0.56, 95%CI [0.42, 0.73], pFDR < .001) community target intentions at S3.

text.text: Higher BAS scores were associated with fewer prosocial community target intentions at S3 (OR = 0.95, 95%CI [0.91, 0.98], pFDR = .015), and higher BIS scores with fewer antisocial community target intentions at S3 (OR = 0.91, 95%CI [0.86, 0.97], pFDR = .040).

Poorer mental health was associated with fewer prosocial community target intentions at S3 (OR = 0.46, 95%CI [0.35, 0.61], pFDR < .001).

text.text: Similarly, participants with secondary education showed fewer antisocial community target intentions than those with tertiary education at S1 (OR = 0.06, 95%CI [0.03, 0.12], pFDR < .001) and S2 (OR = 0.08, 95%CI [0.04, 0.18], pFDR < .001).
